sections.origins_and_history: Dance references in Jewish history date back to the Bible and Talmud, which contain over 30 distinct dance terms. During the dispersion, national community dancing ceased until the halutzim (pioneers) of the First, Second, and Third Aliyahs (1882–1923) reintroduced dances brought from the Diaspora, establishing the horah as the national dance. Choreographer Rivka Sturman created over 90 dances between 1942 and 1983 to provide children with indigenous cultural reflections. Gurit Kadman organized the first First Fruits pageant at kibbutz Dalia in 1944, establishing regular festivals. The Karmiel Dance Festival, launched in 1988, is now Israel's largest dance celebration.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dances feature fixed choreographies matched to specific musical pieces selected by a yotzer (choreographer). Formations include circles, couples, trios, short lines, and group line formations. Movement is highly varied, incorporating the Tza'ad Temani, Horah, and dabke. The pioneer horah was performed at a breakneck pace with dancers linking arms over each other's shoulders.
sections.music_and_instruments: Dances are usually performed to songs in Hebrew, traditional klezmer music, and other popular Israeli genres, archetypally represented by Hava Nagila.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dances are performed publicly in towns and cities, notably on beachfronts and promenades (tayelets), as well as at kibbutzim, festivals, and communal gatherings.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Created to help build a new Israeli culture and celebrate the pioneering spirit, dances are performed at life-cycle events like weddings and bar/bat mitzvahs, holiday celebrations such as Shavuot, and regular weekly recreational sessions.
sections.notable_figures: Rivka Sturman created over 90 classic Israeli dances between 1942 and 1983. Gurit Kadman organized the first Shavuot dance pageant and folk dance festival at kibbutz Dalia in 1944. Baruch Agadati introduced the horah to the Mandate of Palestine in 1924.
sections.regional_variants: Influences include the European Hora, Hasidic dance traditions, the Middle Eastern Arabic dabke, and Yemenite steps. Newer dances incorporate jazz and disco formats, such as Yo Ya and Zodiak.
sections.lineage: Rooted in Diaspora folk dances brought by pioneers (including the horah, polka, Krakowiak, Czerkassiya, and rondo) combined with Middle Eastern and Jewish religious dance traditions.

sections.origins_and_history: Ukusina originates from the coastal region of South Africa among the Zulu people. It has been passed down primarily through oral traditions, with specific historical origins not well-documented. It is currently preserved through cultural programs and festivals like the Zulu Reed Dance.

sections.music_and_instruments: The music is based on the rhythmic beat of traditional Zulu drums and other percussion instruments. A song leader sings interlocking word phrases to guide the performance.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear intricate beadwork, animal skin skirts (such as cow or goat), and feathers. Men may wear an ibheshu or isikhakha, while women may wear an isidwaba. Feathers are used in headpieces and armbands for spiritual significance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Ukusina is performed at weddings, memorial services, and coming-of-age ceremonies. It serves as a way to communicate with ancestors and request their blessings and protection.

claims.text: Ukusina is a traditional dance that has its roots in South Africa's coastal region.
Ukusina dancers kick their legs in any direction up and out, and then stamp each foot into the ground.
The induna, a competent dancer who sets the pace and directs the other dancers, usually leads the dance.
Feathers are thought to link dancers to ancestor spirits, requesting their blessings and presence during the performance.
It is performed during significant festivals, ceremonies, and rites of passage, such as weddings, memorial services, and coming-of-age ceremonies.
The dancers frequently move in line or circular patterns while keeping time with the music and rhythm.

claims.text: Bwola, also known as Acholi bwola, is a traditional dance that originates from the Acholi people in Northern Uganda.
It is reserved for special occasions and performances in front of royalty, including kings and chiefs.
The dancers move in a circular motion, with the men moving in a clockwise direction and the women moving in an anti-clockwise direction.
Bwola is recognized by its distinct elements such as calabash called "Larakaraka" and a cylindrical drum known as "Jagi".

Dancers adorn themselves in traditional attire, including an ostrich-feather headdress, a white cloth elegantly draped around their waist, and ankle bells that add a rhythmic touch to their movements.
The practice of Bwola has encountered challenges, including the prohibition of specific animal parts that are crucial to the dance, thus posing a threat to its cultural preservation.

claims.text: Umxhentso is the traditional dancing of Xhosa people performed mostly by Amagqirha, the traditional healers/Sangoma.

sections.origins_and_history: The Ayyalah originated as a Bedouin war dance performed after tribal victories. It historically served as a ritual for tribal unity when groups were threatened by enemies. In 2014, it was recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves two rows of men facing each other. Participants carry bamboo sticks, swords, or rifles. They move their heads and sticks synchronously with the drum rhythm while hopping from one foot to another. Women participate in the naash ritual, tossing their hair.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes. The melody consists of seven tones in an irregular repeated pattern.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men wear the traditional white dishdasha. Women wear traditional dresses. The dance is performed in open spaces during weddings, national celebrations, and official state visits.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed for weddings, national holidays, state visits, and football matches. It signifies tribal solidarity, victory, and the protection of the community.
sections.notable_figures: The lead performer is typically an inherited role responsible for training other dancers.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include the Razfah, Al-Harbiyya, Al-Wahabbiyya, and the Ardah. Omani versions feature a specific swaying movement to simulate a camel's head.
sections.lineage: The dance descends from Bedouin tribal war traditions and pearl diving celebrations.

claims.text: The yowlah, or Al Ayyala dance, involves dance, drum music, and chanted poetry; its routine is meant to simulate a battle scene.
Two rows of about twenty men face each other, carrying thin sticks of bamboo to signify spears or swords.
The yowlah is recorded (as al-ayyala) on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage Items of Humanity in November 2014.
The yowlah originated as a Bedouin war dance where men would spin rifles after victory in a battle.
In the United Arab Emirates, girls wearing traditional dresses stand at the front, tossing their long hair from side to side.
In Oman the dancers arrange themselves in two rows facing each other and moving forward, swaying back and forth to simulate the head of a moving camel.

sections.origins_and_history: Originating with the Ndau people of Zimbabwe, the dance historically served as a preparation and celebration for warriors. It has evolved into a presentational dance for community gatherings and cultural festivals.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced in a cow horn formation, the performance involves synchronized foot-stomping, rhythmic clapping, and whistling. It progresses from a solo introduction (Mungeneso) to group choreography (chibhubhubhu) and individual displays (chigiyo).
sections.music_and_instruments: The music relies on rhythmic drumming and vocal singing. Women provide the vocal accompaniment and rhythmic clapping to support the male dancers.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men wear mbikiza, vests, feathers or ngututu, and leg/arm ornaments (zvihlabvu/machoba). Women wear colored miniskirts (chikisa), beads (matimwa), and head coverings (maqeyo).
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed at weddings, chief installations, harvest festivals, and burials of royals. It is a secular dance used for entertainment and cultural celebration.
sections.notable_figures: Wilson Kumbula, Enock Porusingazi, Marcia Moyana, and Phillip Kusasa are credited with organizing galas and festivals that sustained the dance.
sections.regional_variants: Known as Muchongolo among the Tsonga (Shangani) people.
sections.lineage: A traditional Ndau dance, with variants found among the Tsonga people.

claims.text: Muchongoyo is a presentational dance and drumming style that emphasizes acrobatic and stomping sequences to dazzle spectators during gatherings or competitions with a complementary rythme of sharp claps.
The word Muchongoyo comes from the Ndau word kuchongoya, which means to stamp one's foot.
The purpose of the violent foot stomping in muchongoyo is historically to chastise warriors before battle and to celebrate success afterward.
A lead guy known as chikopo performs a solo introductory act known as Mungeneso to introduce the dance.

The dancers perform while wearing traditional attire, which for men includes mbikiza and vests on the body, either ngututu or feathers on the head, zvihlabvu or machoba on the legs and arms, and manyatera (sandals) on the feet.
Muchongolo is the name of it in Tsonga.
Muchongoyo is a traditional dance that is performed for celebratory purposes or events of cultural significance such as burials of chief and royals.

sections.origins_and_history: Ekikibi originated among the Bakonzo, a Bantu ethnic community inhabiting the Rwenzori mountain range spanning western Uganda and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, predominantly across Kasese, Bundibugyo, Bunyangabu, and Ntoroko districts. The dance was conceived through the close observation and admiration of fish swimming in mountain streams, translating aquatic locomotion into human choreography. Influenced over centuries by the alpine environment and cultural practices of the Rwenzori heights, Ekikibi has been transmitted across generations as an emblem of Bakonzo identity.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by an ensemble usually consisting of four men and four women arrayed in concentric circles, with the men charting an outer path and women holding the inner ring. Performers execute rhythmic steps, vertical jumps, twists, and complete turns designed to mimic the agile motion of fish in water. As the concentric formations rotate, the dancers continuously exchange focused eye contact and expressive hand gestures to convey emotional intimacy, affection, and mutual joy.
sections.music_and_instruments: Ekikibi is accompanied by vocal love songs specifically composed to praise the character and union of the bride and groom. The instrumental backing is anchored by drums providing percussive cadence, supplemented by rattles for sharp rhythmic texture and flutes carrying melodic phrases. The interplay of instruments supports the undulating tempo required for the dancers' twists, turns, and jumps.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is performed in festive outdoor village clearings, ceremonial reception spaces, or wedding venues across the Rwenzori foothills. Performers wear vibrant, colorful traditional costumes accompanied by decorative adornments that highlight the visual flair of rapid turns and aquatic mimicry.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Staged principally during weddings and communal festive gatherings, Ekikibi celebrates love, marriage, and domestic happiness. It articulates harmony and mutual respect between bride and groom as well as their respective families. In addition to social celebration, the dance honors ancestors and deities, invoking their blessings and spiritual protection over the newly forged marital union.

sections.regional_variants: not described in sources
sections.lineage: A Bantu cultural tradition preserved within Bakonzo communities across Kasese, Bundibugyo, Bunyangabu, and Ntoroko in Uganda and contiguous areas of eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, transmitted through family and community lines during wedding rituals.

basic_steps: Inner-outer circle formation setup: four women form the center circle facing outward, four men form an exterior concentric ring facing inward.
Rhythmic forward traveling step maintaining the circular trajectory around the space.
Aquatic torso twist: rotating the upper body from side to side to simulate swimming motions.
Elevation jump: executing small vertical jumps accented by percussive drum hits.
Turn and focus: performing a sharp pivot or full spin while re-establishing direct eye contact with the dancing partner.
teaching.formation: Concentric circles with four men moving on the outside and four women on the inside.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners must coordinate the circular pathway while sustaining active eye contact and mirroring partner turns across the inner and outer rings.

claims.text: Ekikibi is a traditional love dance of the Bakonzo people.
The Bakonzo reside in the Rwenzori Mountains of western Uganda and eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Bakonzo communities occupy the districts of Kasese, Bundibugyo, Bunyangabu, and Ntoroko.
Ekikibi is performed during weddings and festive events to express marital affection.
The choreography is inspired by the movement of fish in water.
Ekikibi groups typically consist of four men and four women in colorful dress.
The performance is supported by love songs alongside drums, flutes, and rattles.
Dancers arrange themselves in concentric circles with men on the outside and women on the inside.
The dance integrates steps, jumps, twists, and turns mimicking aquatic motion.
Dancers exchange gestures and eye contact to convey romantic emotion.
The ritual honors ancestors and deities for protection and marital blessing.

sections.origins_and_history: The ballet-féerie originated in Russia as a synthesis of the French féerie theatrical genre and the Italian ballo grande dance style. It evolved from a long history of European spectacle, including the Renaissance ballet de cour and 17th-century pièces à machines, which relied on the engineering of architects like Nicola Sabbatini. In the 19th century, these influences merged with the Russian interest in narrative ballet, creating a genre that prioritized visual transformation and ensemble performance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Technique not described in sources. The genre is noted for prioritizing ensemble dances and shifting stage pictures over individual solo virtuosity.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music of the ballet-féerie is characterized by its symphonic scale and ability to support narrative transformations. Tchaikovsky’s works are the primary examples, utilizing full orchestral arrangements to underscore the magical and supernatural elements of the plot.
sections.costume_and_setting: Settings were defined by lavish, mechanically worked stage effects including trapdoors, smoke machines, and quickly changeable sets. Costumes were designed to be brilliant and dazzling, often representing supernatural creatures like gnomes, witches, and fairies to heighten the moral tone of the production.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The ballet-féerie served as a popular, often commercialized form of entertainment that aimed to provide a 'dreamlike' experience for the audience. It functioned as a morality play, depicting the triumph of good over evil through the use of magic talismans and supernatural intervention.
sections.notable_figures: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky is the most significant figure associated with the genre, having composed The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker within this framework.
sections.regional_variants: The genre originated in France as a theatrical 'fairy play' (féerie) before being adapted into the Russian 'ballet-féerie.' Other variants include the English 'fairy extravaganza' and the Spanish 'comedia de magia.'
sections.lineage: The genre descends from the French féerie and the Italian ballo grande, serving as a precursor to modern spectacular stage productions.

sections.origins_and_history: Orunyege-Ntogoro originated in the pre-colonial era within the Bunyoro-Kitara and Tooro kingdoms of western Uganda. Historically, young people gathered under the moonlight to socialize, celebrate communal identity, and express romantic affection. The dance is an intentional synthesis of two distinct traditions: Orunyege, an acrobatic and energetic dance originating in Hoima and Fort Portal districts, and Ntogoro, a graceful, elegant style hailing from Masindi district. According to oral tradition, community elders organized public dance competitions when multiple suitors sought the hand of the same bride. The contest tested physical stamina and resilience, eliminating the first man to tire under the premise that an enduring dancer was best equipped to sustain a household through droughts or famine.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance is carried out by two distinct groups: male dancers known as abakwongezi and female dancers known as abakwetegerezi. The ensemble shifts dynamically across circular, linear, and paired formations under the direction of a master of ceremonies (omukama) and musical cues from the lead drummers. Dancers execute synchronized sequences punctuated by individual demonstrations of virtuosity, including high leaps, rapid spinning, and full-body shaking. Male dancers maintain sharp, percussive leg work that sounds their dried gourd leg rattles in strict alignment with drum rhythms. Female dancers execute smooth, coordinated footwork while using bead or cowrie-shell waist rings to accentuate isolated hip movements, balancing vigorous athleticism with elegant poise.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical foundation of Orunyege-Ntogoro relies on a live ensemble of drums, flutes, and xylophones. The drummers drive the performance, altering tempo, intensity, and rhythmic phrasing to steer the dancers through varying phases of endurance. Flutists and xylophonists weave melodic phrases and harmonies over the drum lines. The music is augmented acoustically by the dancers themselves: the ebinyege leg rattles worn by male dancers produce crisp rhythmic accompaniment with every footfall. The entire sonic environment is directed by the omukama, a master of ceremonies who leads the ensemble with sung chants, praise poetry, and humorous spoken banter.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes are designed to serve both acoustic and visual functions. Male dancers wear shirts and shorts, leaving the lower legs free to securely fasten ebinyege, which are rattles fashioned from dried gourds or calabashes. Female dancers wear long skirts and blouses, accented around the hips by entogoro—ornamental rings crafted from beads or cowrie shells that magnify the sway and rotation of the pelvis. Historically danced outdoors on bare earth in evening moonlight, the tradition is now commonly staged in school halls, cultural festivals, tourism venues, and ceremonial grounds.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally functioning as a primary courtship ritual, Orunyege-Ntogoro allowed young adults of the Bunyoro and Tooro communities to evaluate prospective partners on the basis of physical endurance, agility, and grace. It continues to be an integral part of traditional weddings, initiation rites, and Empaako naming ceremonies, as well as seasonal community celebrations. Ethnomusicologist Linda Cimardi notes that runyege serves as a vital medium for staging local culture, reinforcing traditional gender norms while also offering performers a space to negotiate personal expression.
sections.notable_figures: Ethnomusicologist Linda Cimardi has documented runyege as a wide performance genre encompassing singing, instrumentation, dance, and acting in western Uganda.
sections.regional_variants: The dance unites two distinct regional styles of western Uganda: the Orunyege component, which developed in the Hoima and Fort Portal districts and is known for its intense, athletic, and acrobatic character; and the Ntogoro component, which emerged from Masindi district and is defined by graceful, elegant movements.
sections.lineage: Orunyege-Ntogoro belongs to the runyege performance genre of the Banyoro and Batooro peoples, rooted in the heritage of the Bunyoro-Kitara and Tooro kingdoms.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance dates back to the pre-colonial era of the Bunyoro and Tooro kingdoms. It originated as a social and ceremonial practice where young people gathered under the moonlight to socialize and compete for partners. Historically, it was a courtship contest where elders used the dance to select suitable husbands based on their physical endurance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform in groups of men (abakwongezi) and women (abakwetegerezi). The movement involves energetic leg shaking by men to sound their rattles and graceful hip movements by women to accentuate their waist rings. Formations include circles, lines, and pairs, with specific moments for individual improvisation such as spinning and jumping.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by a master of ceremonies (omukama) who sings and chants. Musical instruments include drums, which set the rhythmic patterns, as well as flutes and xylophones that provide melodic layers. The ebinyege leg rattles worn by men act as a percussive instrument played through movement.
sections.costume_and_setting: Male dancers wear shorts and shirts with dried gourd rattles (ebinyege) tied to their legs. Female dancers wear long skirts and blouses with beaded or cowrie shell rings (entogoro) around their waists. Performances traditionally took place outdoors in community spaces, but are now common on formal stages and at cultural festivals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Beyond courtship, Entogoro is performed during weddings, initiation rites, and Empaako naming ceremonies. It symbolizes cultural identity, physical prowess, and the social expectations of marriage. It serves as a tool for cultural education, passing down traditional knowledge to younger generations.
sections.notable_figures: The performance is led by the omukama (master of ceremonies), who directs the dancers and audience. Ethnomusicologist Linda Cimardi has documented the dance as a medium for staging local culture and negotiating gender expression in western Uganda.
sections.regional_variants: The genre is a combination of Orunyege from Hoima and Fort Portal, which is more acrobatic, and Ntogoro from Masindi, which is noted for its grace and elegance.
sections.lineage: Entogoro is a subclass of Ugandan folk dance, specifically belonging to the Batooro and Banyoro ethnic groups. it is part of the wider 'runyege' performance genre which includes music, dance, and acting.

sections.origins_and_history: Naleyo is rooted among the Karamajong people, an agro-pastoral ethnic group living in North Eastern Uganda who speak the Nilotic language NgaKarimojong. The dance functions as an annual post-harvest custom, emerging from seasonal rhythms to provide a structured gathering for celebration and social bonding.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in two parallel lines with women in one line and men arranged in the opposite line facing one another. Dancers face each other across the divide and execute energetic, high vertical jumps. In this setting, women actively choose their male dancing partners as the two lines interact.
sections.music_and_instruments: Accompaniment is provided by traditional instruments, specifically the adungu (arched harp), the ngoma (drum), and the ekitirikiti (shakers or percussive instruments). These instruments supply the melodic and rhythmic backdrop that drives the dancers' repeated vertical leaps.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men wear traditional attire including a headdress made of animal skin, an animal hide skirt, and a beaded belt. Women dress in an animal hide skirt and beaded necklaces. The dance is held outdoors during the post-harvest period in North Eastern Uganda.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Naleyo is held annually after the harvest season as a wooing and courtship celebration. It provides a recognized cultural venue for young men and women to find love and select suitors, while serving as a broader expression of Karamajong cultural heritage.

sections.origins_and_history: The folk dances of the Khiamniungan Naga tribe originate from Nagaland in northeast India. They are deeply rooted in the cultural identity of the people, traditionally marking historical practices such as headhunting raids, peace treaties, agricultural cycles, and communal feasts of merit.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances vary by context, ranging from the backward-moving steps of the Shapautaithiu welcome dance to the vigorous combat leaps of the Kheulak ritual where warriors jump over grounded Dao swords. Pre-war dances involve men mimicking wild animals with high-pitched shouts, while festival dances incorporate communal singing.
sections.music_and_instruments: Musical accompaniment relies primarily on vocal chants, songs, and high-pitched battle cries, reflecting the ceremonial and martial heritage of the community.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers appear fully dressed in traditional attire including the Ahangküha, combat armor, and traditional weapons such as spears, shields, and Dao swords. Settings include the anterior of the main Morung and festival grounds during community celebrations.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dances are performed during major festivals like Miu, Tsoukum, and Khaozaosie-Hok-Ah, as well as during feasts of merit, peace treaty receptions, pre-war preparations, and post-victory returns.

sections.origins_and_history: Ekitaguriro originates from the Nkore or Ankole region in southwestern Uganda. The Ankole kingdom was formed through the amalgamation of the Nkore kingdom with the smaller chiefdoms of Sheema, Buhweju, and Igara, comprising the Bahima (nobles and pastoralists) and Bairu (agriculturalists and peasants) factions.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance begins with Okwevuga, a form of poetry where men narrate their life achievements. Following this, men imitate walking cows by stepping from one leg to another, while women sway from side to side with hands spread across and above their heads to represent long-horned cattle.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music and sound are produced using flutes, the Engalabi, shakers, drums, and the clapping of hands.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear traditional dancewear called 'bitambi' or 'lessu' tied around the waist with a lighter cloth draped over the shoulders. Women wear African-themed jewelry, and men add shackle-like beads to draw attention to foot movements.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Ekitaguriro is a celebratory dance expressing gratitude for cattle and showcasing local prosperity during social gatherings, births, marriages, and abundant harvests, symbolizing the cultural significance of cattle.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is influenced by the Natha Pantha tradition. It is a long-standing practice of the Arebhahse community in Sullia, performed during the Suggi month.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers move from house to house, dancing around a central lamp. The Sanyasi character roams the courtyard independently, interacting with the public using provocative language. The group chants 'Ḍimbisāle' while moving between locations.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music includes singing and the use of a conch and drum, particularly by the Dasayya character. The primary vocal element is the chanting of 'Ḍimbisāle' and specific ritual songs.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes vary by character: the Sanyasi wears dried camouflage leaves and a wooden phallus; the Dasayya wears a white dhoti, red shawl, and Mundasu; the Bhatru wears a sacred thread and sandalwood paste; the Koraga is covered in dark paint; the Byari wears a white banyan and traditional hat.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed during the full moon of the Suggi month. It is a religious ritual involving prayers to Kadri Manjunatha and local spirits, serving as a form of mythological mimicry.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in the 1920s within African American communities in the Carolinas. It was initially a 'street dance' before being standardized by Arthur Murray studios in the late 1930s. It was known by various names such as 'flea hop' and 'Florida Hop' before 'Collegiate Shag' became the standard term in the late 20th century.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance uses a six-count basic step: slow (step-hop), slow (step-hop), quick (step), quick (step). Partners remain in a close, offset, chest-to-chest position. The lead's right hand is on the follow's back, and the follow's left arm is on the lead's shoulder or neck. Arms are often held high.
sections.music_and_instruments: Performed to uptempo swing, pre-swing jazz, Dixieland, and Gypsy-Jazz. The music is characterized by a high tempo, typically 185–250+ beats per minute.

sections.origins_and_history: Tambor de Crioula has roots in the 19th century, with the earliest known reference dating to 1818. It served as a space for resistance and identity among enslaved Africans. It was officially registered as Brazilian Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2007.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance occurs in a circle. Women dance individually in the center, moving their entire bodies in harmony with the rhythm. The 'punga' (belly bump) is used to invite a new dancer into the center. Men play the drums and lead the singing.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is driven by the 'parelha,' a set of three drums (crivador, meião, and roncador) made from hollowed logs and animal skin. Pandeiros and matracas are also used. The drums are tuned by fire.
sections.costume_and_setting: Women wear wide, colorful printed skirts, lace-trimmed petticoats, and blouses, often with turbans and jewelry. Men wear white trousers, straw hats, and printed shirts. It is performed in squares, terreiros, or during festivals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It is performed for Saint Benedict, as well as for birthdays, football victories, and community gatherings. It is a social and religious expression of Afro-Brazilian identity.
sections.notable_figures: not described in sources
sections.regional_variants: Variations exist in the interior of Maranhão, including men dancing in a side circle with movements similar to capoeira.
sections.lineage: Linked to other Maranhão traditions such as bumba-meu-boi and cacuriá.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated during the Edo period, influenced by the dances of visiting sailors. By the middle of the eighteenth century, it had become a performance showcase for local girls. In 1976, the Japanese government designated it as an intangible cultural heritage, and in 2009, it was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, later being incorporated into the Furyu-odori category in 2022.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Ten to twenty girls, aged 5 to 12, perform in two rows facing each other or in a circle. They hold bamboo strips in their hands and strike them together to create a rhythmic sound. The dancers are accompanied by an a cappella choir of older women.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is provided entirely by an a cappella choir of five to ten older women. The only instrumental element is the rhythmic clicking of bamboo strips held by the dancers, which produces the signature sound of the performance.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dancers wear colorful kimono. The performance takes place on January 15th at local shrines or in front of houses within the community in Miura, Japan.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed to celebrate the New Year and to invoke good fortune, specifically targeting prosperity and abundant fishing catches for the community.

claims.text: Chakkirako is a dance performed at a festival in Miura, Japan, to celebrate the New Year and bring good fortune, especially in fishing.
In 2009, it was inscribed in UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and in 2022, it was incorporated into the broader subject of Furyu-odori.
The dance originated in the Edo period with influences by the dances of visiting sailors.
Every year in the middle of January, ten to twenty girls in colorful kimono between the ages of 5 and 12 perform the dance at a shrine or in front of houses.
They are accompanied by five to ten older women singing a capella.
The dancers hold bamboo strips in their hands and strike them together, which produces the sound that gives the dance its name.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in the 16th century under Ratu Melinting II in Lampung. It was historically a private royal ritual until it was refined in 1958 and renamed from 'Cetik Kipas' to 'Melinting' by President Sukarno in 1965.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves eight performers, four men and four women. The performance is divided into four rounds: opening, kugowo queen, floating kenui, and closing. Specific footwork, posture, and counts are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music utilizes traditional Lampung instruments including Kalo Bala, kendang, gongs, gamelan, and fiddle. The music serves to accompany the entrance of dancers and signal respect for guests.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men wear tapis cloth, belanga shirts, seretei feathers, gold skullcaps, and fans. Women wear tapis pepadun, white kebaya, yellow veils, jukum fruit, ruwi bracelets, and fans. Make-up is essential to the performance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed at traditional events to welcome guests. It symbolizes gratitude for happiness and the majesty of the Melinting kingdom.
sections.notable_figures: Ratu Melinting II (creator) and President Sukarno (who renamed the dance).
sections.regional_variants: not described in sources
sections.lineage: The dance is a relic of the Melinting Kingdom and is associated with the development of Islam in the region.

claims.text: The Melinting dance is a traditional dance from Lampung province, Indonesia, which existed in the sixteenth century.
The dance was renamed Melinting at the request of President Sukarno in 1965.
The dance was created by Ratu Melinting II and served to show gratitude and the majesty of the kingdom.
The dance is performed by eight dancers, four men and four women, divided into four rounds.
The dance uses various musical instruments including Kalo Bala, kendang, gongs, gamelan, and fiddle.
Before 1958, the dance was exclusively owned by the royal family.

sections.origins_and_history: Originating in the North Caucasus, these dances reflect the martial history and Nart Epic mythology of the Circassian people. Historically, they served as physical training and social etiquette, with competition styles like Islamey used to demonstrate character and endurance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dances are divided into Wuj (circle), Qafa (partner), and Islamey (fast-paced). Men dance on their toes with hands often behind their backs; women glide with motionless upper bodies. Partners maintain a respectful distance, especially in Qafa, where touching is prohibited.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is led by the pshine (accordion), accompanied by pkhachich (wood blocks), bereban (drum), and the shichepshin (fiddle). Rhythms are often in 4/4 or 8/4 time, with specific pieces like Sheshen using off-beat bellows-pulling techniques.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men wear the 'cherkes', a military coat with bullet cartridges, often carrying a dagger. Women wear traditional attire that allows for gliding movements. Performances occur at 'Djegu' gatherings or festivals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dances are performed at weddings, social gatherings, and festivals. They serve as a medium for courtship, social standing, and the preservation of cultural identity in the diaspora.
sections.notable_figures: Hapcha Zaodin (accordionist), Aslan Tlebzu (accordionist), Saeed Bazoqa (composer), and Firas Valentine (musician).
sections.regional_variants: Kabardian (stately/lyrical), Bzhedug (faster/broader), and Mozdok (Hatu dance).
sections.lineage: Influenced the development of Cossack dance; shares roots with Abkhazian traditions.

teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with basic gliding steps; advanced dancers master toe-dancing and sword-dodging imitations.

sections.origins_and_history: The Plinn originated in the Pays Fañch, south of the Côtes-d'Armor. It is a traditional Breton dance that has been practiced for generations within the local fest-noz culture. In 1971, Alan Stivell adapted the traditional air into a rock-influenced piece, which brought the dance and its music to a broader public.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The Plinn is a fast and physical chain dance. Dancers hold the arms of their neighbors and perform two small jumps as part of the rhythmic sequence.
sections.music_and_instruments: Traditional accompaniment includes the biniou (Breton bagpipe) and the bombarde (a double-reed instrument). The music is often accompanied by kan ha diskan, a traditional call-and-response singing style. Modern arrangements, such as those by Alan Stivell, incorporate electric guitar, harp, organ, bass, and percussion.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is traditionally performed at festoù-noz, which are social gatherings in Brittany. No specific costume is described in sources, though it is a traditional folk dance setting.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The Plinn is a social dance performed at community festivals. It is associated with a 'tribal trance' state, achieved through the repetition of a relentless rhythm for hours.
sections.notable_figures: Alan Stivell, Dan Ar Braz, Loeiz Ropars, The Morvan Brothers, Étienne Rivoallan, and Georges Cadoudal.
sections.regional_variants: The Plinn is closely associated with the Pays Fisel, another region with a distinct dance style often performed in similar contexts.
sections.lineage: The Plinn is a traditional Breton folk dance, sharing cultural and musical roots with other Celtic traditions, including those in the Highlands and Donegal.

claims.text: The Plinn dance originates from the Pays Fañch region.
The dance is characterized by its speed and the execution of two small jumps while holding neighbors' arms.
Dancers may enter a 'tribal trance' by repeating the same rhythm for hours.
Alan Stivell transformed the traditional air into a pop song in 1971.
Stivell alternated between dancing and playing the biniou.
The dance features pentatonic themes.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is believed to have originated 2000 years ago as the Llama llama ritual of the Uru civilization in Oruro. During the colonial era, Spanish authorities banned indigenous ceremonies, leading the Uru to conceal their gods behind Christian icons. The god Tiw was transformed into 'El Tío' and the devil of Christian liturgy. The first institutionalized squad, Gran Tradicional y Auténtica Diablada Oruro, was founded in 1904.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is a series of three versions, each consisting of seven moves. It features a confrontation between angels and demons who move continuously in formations like circles and crosses. Demons perform 'kick jumps' (pieds sautés) while the Archangel uses a sword and shield to direct the troop. The choreography requires high coordination to manage the 30kg weight of the costumes.
sections.music_and_instruments: Originally performed with Sikuris (panpipe bands), modern versions use brass orchestras. The music consists of two parts: the March and the Devil's Mecapaqueña. Key instruments in the Peruvian variant include the siku, bass drum, snare drum, cymbals, and triangle.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear monstrous masks with horns and bulging eyes, and heavy capes embroidered with gold thread and multicolored motifs. The Archangel wears a blouse, short skirt, and wings. Settings range from the streets and public squares of Oruro and Puno to indoor theaters.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is the centerpiece of the Carnaval de Oruro and the Fiesta de la Candelaria. It represents the struggle between good and evil, the Seven Deadly Sins, and the syncretic relationship between miners and the spirits of the underworld.
sections.notable_figures: Pedro Pablo Corrales founded the first formal squad in 1904. The Archangel Saint Michael is the lead character, while Lucifer and Satan lead the demonic ranks.
sections.regional_variants: The Diablada Puneña (Peru) includes characters like the 'Old Man' and 'Red Skin' and was influenced by Jesuit autos sacramentales. The Chilean version at Fiesta de La Tirana was influenced by the 'Diablos sueltos' tradition. The Diablada de Píllaro in Ecuador represents a rebellion against the Church.
sections.lineage: Descended from the Uru Llama llama and Aymara rituals to Anchanchu. It has influenced modern festival traditions in Chile (since 1952) and Argentina.

basic_steps: The March: A rhythmic, high-stepping walk used for the entrance.
The Jump: Demons perform explosive, two-footed or alternating kick-jumps.
The Cross: A group formation where lines of dancers intersect.
The Circle: Dancers rotate around a central point, often the Archangel.
The Confrontation: A series of aggressive lunges toward the opposing side.
The Mecapaqueña: A faster, more syncopated footwork sequence.
The Defeat: A kneeling or bowing gesture performed by the devils at the end.
teaching.formation: Two columns (angels vs. demons) led by the Archangel.
teaching.level_notes: Requires extreme physical stamina due to costume weight.

sections.origins_and_history: Pursere Kattuna is a traditional ritualistic dance form performed by Tulu-speaking people from various castes across different parts of Belthangady taluk. It is a living heritage practice of Tulunadu, showcasing the folk imagination of Tulu society and preserving oral narratives, mythic storytelling, and seasonal practices.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The ritual includes acting, singing, dancing, symbolic storytelling and mythological mimicry. Performers interact with each other and with the public during the different stages of the enactment. Technique not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical instruments used in Pursa Kattuna includes Tase, Dolu, Nadaswara, Shruti. These instruments guide the rhythm of the dance, mythic dialogues and singing sequences throughout the night.
sections.costume_and_setting: Pursa Kattuna uses a wide range of costumes and roles representing various castes, professions, mythic figures and social archetypes. Costumes may depict Brahmins, priests, mendicants, ascetics, fortune tellers, Koti Chennaya, wild animals including bears, tiger, lion, monkey, scholars, thieves, ghosts, spiritual entities, and Christian or Muslim characters.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The performance is held during the full moon in the month of Suggi according to the Tulu calendar. Dancers visit the homes of people belonging to different social strata, blessing them with healing, prosperity and protection.
sections.notable_figures: not described in sources
sections.regional_variants: A similar type of performance exists in the Sullia region, but it uses a different costume style known as Siddavesha. The three notable mythic farce characters associated with Siddavesha are Sanyasi, Bhatru and Dasayye.
sections.lineage: The style shows influence from the Natha Pantha spiritual tradition.

claims.text: Pursere Kattuna is a religious and traditional folk dance form of Tulunadu, performed mainly in the villages of Belthangady taluk in the Dakshina Kannada district of Karnataka, India.
The performance is held during the full moon in the month of Suggi according to the Tulu calendar.
Pursa Kattuna takes place from late evening until the early hours of the morning.
The ritual includes acting, singing, dancing, symbolic storytelling and mythological mimicry.
The musical instruments used in Pursa Kattuna includes Tase, Dolu, Nadaswara, Shruti.
Pursere Kattuna is a living heritage practice of Tulunadu, combining ritual healing, traditional belief, humor, performance art and community theatre.

sections.origins_and_history: Jathilan originated in Ponorogo, East Java, Indonesia. Hypotheses regarding its broader development suggest it may have emerged as a ritual reenactment of battle during Prince Diponegoro's war against Dutch colonial forces, or earlier based on Mataram-era troops riding against the Dutch. In East Java, it developed as an integral part of the Reog Ponorogo performance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers dance while straddling flat hobbyhorses made from woven bamboo or rattan. Groups traditionally consist of two to eight dancers who move across a cordoned-off performance space separated from the audience. Dancers portray troops riding horses, executing choreographed riding movements. Unlike rural Jaran Kepang where dancers undergo trance and magic stunts, East Javanese Jathil dancers do not perform trance, walk on coals, or eat glass.
sections.music_and_instruments: Performances are accompanied by traditional musical instruments, including the angklung, gongs, and dog-dog drums. In related regional forms like Balinese Sang Hyang Jaran, the audience may also participate by forming a chorus and singing.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers mount woven bamboo or rattan horses decorated with colorful paints, cloth, beads, and sequins. Costumes feature colorful clothing, occasional soldier uniforms, and small bells strung around the ankles. Costumes appear feminized in comparison to shamans. Performances are held in cordoned-off performance spaces, celebratory family gatherings, or public street settings.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Jathilan and related horse dances are performed to celebrate special life events, such as boys' circumcisions or rites of passage, as well as for public entertainment. The dance portrays troops riding horses and military virility. In modern community settings such as Yogyakarta, Jathilan art associations like Turonggo Wiro Budoyo serve as active social gathering spaces for local youth.
sections.notable_figures: Turonggo Wiro Budoyo (TWB) is an active jathilan art association based in the Wirobrajan district of Yogyakarta.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is known as Kuda Lumping in West Java, Jaran Kepang in Central Java, Jathilan in East Java, and Sang Hyang Jaran in Bali. Among the Javanese diaspora in Suriname, Malaysia, and Singapore, it is known as Kuda Kepang.
sections.lineage: Jathilan belongs to the broader Javanese hobbyhorse dance tradition and is specifically embedded within the Reog Ponorogo performance tradition of East Java.

claims.text: Jathilan originated in Ponorogo, East Java, Indonesia, and portrays horsemen.
Dancers ride flat horses made of woven bamboo decorated with paint and cloth.
One hypothesis connects the dance's origin to Diponegoro's war against Dutch colonial forces.
In East Java, the dance is called Jathilan and constitutes a portion of the Reog Ponorogo performance.
A Jathil is a youthful horseman riding a woven bamboo horse who does not perform trances or stunts.
Traditionally danced by gemblakan, the Jathil is today typically performed by female dancers.
Performances are accompanied by traditional instruments including angklung, gongs, and dog-dog drums.
Turonggo Wiro Budoyo is an active jathilan art association operating in Yogyakarta.

sections.origins_and_history: Moraego originated among the highland peoples of Central Sulawesi as a ritual circle dance performed at major precolonial ceremonies to communicate with pre-Christian deities and promote fertility and agriculture. European missionaries and Dutch authorities documented it in the late 19th century, noting its religious and social significance and attempting to curtail its practice.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Moraego is performed as a circle dance with men and unmarried women dancing in close physical contact. Married women and children are spectators. The dance includes singing in Uma raego language and trance-like chanting. Specific footwork, arm movements, and tempo are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by songs in the Uma raego language, including trance-like chanting used for healing. Specific instruments are not described in the sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Moraego is performed at major rituals including puberty rites and agricultural ceremonies. It serves to communicate with deities, promote fertility, and heal sickness. During puberty rites, adults celebrate with Moraego while children are secluded and fed rice porridge. Animal sacrifices accompany the rites.
sections.notable_figures: Adriani and Kruyt witnessed Moraego in 1897 in Kulawi. Captain Boonstra van Heerdt recorded performances in Kulawi, Lindu, and other locations.
sections.regional_variants: Moraego is known among various Toradja groups including Palu Toradja, Koro Toradja, Poso Toradja, Mori District, and Saadang Toradja, indicating regional variants within Central Sulawesi.
sections.lineage: Moraego is a traditional Indonesian dance rooted in pre-Christian ritual practices of Central Sulawesi highlanders, with influences from local animist beliefs and social customs.

claims.text: Moraego (or raego, or marego), is the name of a traditional and ritual dance in Central Sulawesi.
In historical time, Central Sulawesi highlanders have performed circle dances and accompanying songs (in Uma raego) at all major precolonial rituals.
The Moraego dances and songs were performed to summon and communicate with their pre-Christian deities.
Missionaries, as well as Dutch authorities, sought to reduce the moraego performances for various reasons.
Married women did not dance the raego, although they and their children were audience to these public events.
From the end of the 19th century there are several descriptions of the Moraego dances and rituals, especially from the Palu Toradja, the Koro Toradja, as well as the Poso Toradja.
In 1897 Adriani and Kruyt witnessed a raego in Kulawi on their journey across Central Sulawesi.
Some types included trance-like chanting that was meant to heal and cure sickness.
While the children were confined to heal and fed only rice porridge after the puberty rites, adults celebrated just outside the temple singing and dancing moraego every night.
One animal was sacrificed for every girl and for every three to five boys.

claims.text: Gulikan Theyyam is worshipped in Kerala and is important in Kerala astrology as son of Shani deva.
Gulikan Theyyam is part of the Kaliyattam, a popular religious folk dance in the Indian state of Kerala.
In the Tulu Nadu region this deity is worshipped as Guliga Daiva, a lord in Hindu Culture.
Gulikan is worshipped in small shrines called Gulikan Kavus.
The most famous and powerful one is at Nileshwar in the district of Kasaragod and is popularly known as the Benkanakavu [Veeranakavu].
The adjacent Koroth Nair Tharavadu, Kazhakakkar, and Kolakkar organize the Theyyam festival in Benanakavu once every two years.
A temple named Pattare Paradevatha Kshethram performs Gulikan Theyyam annually.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originates from the Udupi and Dakshina Kannada regions of Karnataka and is performed by the Mundaala community. It is a spiritual practice conducted during the full moon of the Tulu month of Mai to invoke protection from disease and evil.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform in a circle, with 5 to 12 members per group. The performance involves heavy, colorful costumes made from coconut and palm leaves, face paint, and a central masked dancer representing Koragajja. The movement is accompanied by drumming and singing.

sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear heavy, colorful dresses constructed from tender coconut and palm leaves. The masked dancer representing Koragajja uses black body paint. The performance takes place in village settings, including house visits and processions to the village outskirts.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed during the seven-day Kangilu Kunitha, the dance is a ritual to propitiate goddess Khadgeshwari and the spirit Koragajja. It aims to foster peace, harmony, and community spirit while protecting the village from negative energy.

claims.text: Kangeelu or Kangilu is a traditional folk dance from Udupi and Dakshina Kannada region in the South Indian state of Karnataka.
It is a spiritual dance performed on the full moon day in Mai month of Tulu calendar, corresponding to March in the Gregorian calendar.
The dance is generally performed by the mundaala community living in Udupi and Dakshina Kannada.
There are 5 to 12 members in each group and the dancers dress and decorate themselves similarly and stand in a circle.
The dancers wear heavy and colorful dresses as well as face paint.
Amidst the dancing, a dancer appears wearing a mask and black paint smeared across the body imitating the spirit god Koragajja and dances in a unique way to draw the attention of the people.
The dance is performed as a part of a seven day Kangilu Kunitha to propitiate the goddess Khadgeshwari and Koragajja, a spirit considered as a form of god Shiva.

sections.origins_and_history: Haitian dance originated from a blend of African, European, and indigenous Taíno influences during the colonial period of Saint-Domingue (1501–1804). Early dances like Méringue emerged from creolisation, combining African rhythms and European ballroom elements. The Catholic Church opposed African-derived dances, labeling practitioners as black magic. After independence in 1804, dance celebrated freedom and national identity, with battle dances commemorating revolutionary victories. The US occupation introduced American music and dance styles, while the Négritude Movement in the 1930s affirmed Black identity and brought Haitian dance to wider attention. Under Duvalier's regime, dance festivals served both cultural pride and political distraction. Modern Haitian dance continues to evolve, incorporating global influences and preserving traditional forms.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Haitian dance includes diverse styles with varied formations and movements. Méringue is a partner ballroom dance with a slower tempo and string-based orchestration, featuring graceful, flowing movements. Kontradans involves four couples performing fast-paced figures without touching, exchanging places in patterns called '8'. Vodou ritual dances like Rada feature slow, undulating, snake-like body movements, while Petro rites are fiery and aggressive. Battle dances such as Karabiyen are choreographed couples dances. Kompa is danced mostly in pairs with close, expressive ballroom elements. Technique details are specific to each style; beginners often start with basic footwork and rhythm familiarization. Overall, Haitian dance emphasizes rhythm, coordinated group movement, and cultural expression.
sections.music_and_instruments: Haitian dance music features a mix of African-derived rhythms and European instrumentation. Méringue uses string instruments like guitar and banjo, saxophone, trap drums, and Congo drums. Vodou dances rely on polyrhythmic drumming with drums, rattles, bells, and conch shell trumpets. Rara festival music includes drums, maracas, bamboo trumpets (vaksen), and bells. Kompa combines electric guitar, horns, vocals, and drums, evolving from Méringue and incorporating jazz and Cuban influences. Rabòday and Rasin music fuse traditional rhythms with modern electronic sounds and rap. The music is integral to the dance, setting tempo, mood, and movement cues.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes vary by dance style and occasion. Vodou ritual dances feature vibrant, symbolic costumes reflecting spirits and rites, often including masks and specific colors. Battle dances and folk troupes wear attire linked to their historical or social context. Méringue and Kompa dancers typically wear elegant ballroom or social dance clothing. Dance settings range from street festivals like Rara processions to formal theater performances by ballet folklorique companies. Celebrations such as Carnaval des Fleurs and Koudyay festivals provide communal spaces for dance expression.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dance in Haiti serves religious, social, and political functions. Vodou dances are sacred rituals connecting practitioners with spirits and ancestors. Battle dances commemorate revolutionary history and military victories. Social dances like Méringue and Kompa express cultural identity and community bonding. Festivals such as Rara celebrate slave revolution heritage and religious syncretism. Dance also acts as resistance against oppression and a means of uplifting spirits amid hardship, exemplified by the proverb 'Apre Dans, Tanbou Lou' ('After dance, drums are heavy').
sections.notable_figures: Katherine Dunham documented and popularized Haitian dance internationally, integrating it into her choreography and scholarship. Jean-Léon Destiné founded Haiti's national ballet and taught Haitian dance in the US, promoting African Haitian dance forms. Zora Neale Hurston recorded Haitian dance traditions in her 1938 work 'Tell My Horse.' Contemporary groups like Ballet folklorique du Théâtre national d'Haïtienne and Ballet Milokan continue to preserve and innovate Haitian dance.
sections.regional_variants: Vodou dances vary by rite: Rada dances from northern Haiti feature calm, fluid movements; Petro dances from central and southern regions are aggressive and fiery; Gede dances relate to death and fertility, celebrated on All Souls' Day. Folk dances like Kombit troupes perform in rural and urban areas. Kontradans and Tumba Francesca reflect European and African fusion with regional variations. Kompa and Méringue styles differ between elite and proletariat social groups.
sections.lineage: Haitian dance descends from African tribal dances (Kongo, Dahomey, Igbo), European ballroom dances (Contra dance, French court dances), and indigenous Taíno traditions. It evolved through creolisation during colonial times, revolution, and post-independence cultural development. Influences from American jazz, rock, and Caribbean genres shaped modern forms like Kompa and mini-jazz. The Négritude Movement and folklorists like Dunham and Hurston helped document and transmit the tradition globally.

claims.text: The Dance of Haiti is a collection of performing art of the Haitian people's culture, pulling from African, Arawak/Taino, European, and local origins.
Méringue is Haiti's national dance, mixing Haitian elements such as Karabiyen dance and Kongo drum beat, with two versions for elite and proletariat.
Rada rites dances are slow, undulating, snake-like body movements with a calm, fluid tone, representing rhythms from the Dahomey region.
Kompa, created in the 1950s by Nemours Jean-Baptiste, combines merengue, jazz, and Cuban music, danced mostly in pairs with ballroom elements.
Katherine Dunham documented Haitian dance and brought it to mainstream attention, integrating African American, Caribbean, African, and South American styles.
Dance festivals like Koudyay were sponsored by Duvalier as distractions to quell public dissent.

claims.text: Okayama (岡山) is a Japanese kōwaka-mai of the hōgan-mono genre composed in the Muromachi period.
It tells the story of the bereaved relatives of Satō Tsugunobu and Satō Tadanobu, two of Yoshitsune's retainers.
The text of the work has been connected to a passage in the Gikeiki, and it is a sequel to the kōwaka Yashima.
Only one manuscript of the libretto survives: the Bunroku-bon copied by Ueyama Munehisa, held by Tenri Central Library.
At Takadachi, Yoshitsune is asked by Nikō, the mother of his fallen retainers, to act as the eboshi-oya for their children.
The widows become nuns and travel as pilgrims around Mutsu Province until they come to Okayama, where they build a hut and die peacefully together.

sections.origins_and_history: Tsyganochka originated in Russia in the 19th century, evolving from a melody composed by Ivan Vasilievich Vasiliev, director of a Russian Roma choir. The melody 'Gypsy Vengerka' was based on a poem by Apollon Grigoriev, a fan of Romani music. The dance developed without a fixed choreography, becoming popular among Russian Roma choirs and folk performers who added a recognizable refrain. It reflects the influence of Russian Roma musical traditions on Russian folk dance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The common form, 'Tsyganochka with Entrance,' begins with a slow tempo where the dancer walks into the dance area, showing off but without complicated figures. The tempo then gradually accelerates as the dancer warms up and intensifies movements. The dance is typically performed solo, with no fixed choreography, allowing expressive interpretation aligned with the music's tempo changes. Technique not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is in a minor key, unusual for Russian folk dance, and in 4/4 time. The classic melody was composed by Ivan Vasilievich Vasiliev for guitar, inspired by Apollon Grigoriev's poem. The melody became popular with Russian Roma choirs and folk performers. The music features a recognizable refrain often added by folk singers. Instruments mentioned include guitar; other instrumentation is not described.

claims.text: Tsyganochka (Russian: Цыганочка, "Gypsy Girl") is a Russian folk dance stylized under the Russian Roma tunes.
The music is in minor tonality, unusual in Russian folk dance, in 4/4 time signature.
In the common version called "Tsyganochka with Entrance", the tempo is initially slow and then gradually speeds up.
During the slow introduction the dancer walks into the dance area, showing off, but without complicated dance figures and then gradually warms up.
The classic melody of Tsyganochka with Entrance was written in the 19th century by Ivan Vasilievich Vasiliev, director of a Russian Roma choir and composer.

Ivan Vasiliev wrote the melody 'Gypsy Vengerka' for guitar based on a verse by Apollon Grigoriev, a fan of Romani music, which became popular with Russian Roma choirs and based on which a dance evolved without particular choreography.
Folk added the recognizable refrain 'эх раз еще раз еще много-много раз' ('Eh, again, and once more, and many-many more times') into Grigoriev's verse or its variations.
Vladimir Vysotsky performed a song 'Эх, раз, еще раз...' in tsyganochka style in the 1967 film Brief Encounters.

sections.origins_and_history: Salegy originated in the 1950s in northwestern Madagascar as an electrified form of the traditional antsa music performed by Betsimisaraka and Tsimihety peoples during possession rituals. It evolved from Sub-Saharan African folk roots and was modernized with electric guitars and synthesizers. Eusèbe Jaojoby, a Sakalava singer, was a key figure in popularizing salegy internationally.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Salegy dance is energetic and communal, often performed in nightclubs and social gatherings. Women perform the mbiwy dance accompanied by hand rhythms called rombo manofo. The dance matches the rapid tempo and polyrhythmic beat, featuring footwork and intricate hand clapping during the folaka section. Technique not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: Salegy music features ringing electric guitars with high-life style lines, real or synthesized accordion, heavy electric bass, and a percussion section including a Western drum kit, djembe, and shakers. The rhythm is syncopated and polyrhythmic in 6/8 or 12/4 time with accents on the 3rd or 7th beat, typically around 290 BPM. Vocals are polyphonic and call-and-response.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes and settings vary but salegy is commonly heard in nightclubs, cabarets, parties, and dance floors across Madagascar. Traditional dances like mbiwy are performed by women in the north. No specific costume details described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Salegy is performed at social celebrations, nightclubs, and parties throughout Madagascar. It derives from ritual music used in possession rites to invoke spirits but today is a popular dance music form symbolizing Malagasy identity and communal joy.
sections.notable_figures: Eusèbe Jaojoby is known as the 'King of Salegy' and a pioneer of the genre. Other important artists include Ninie Doniah, Vaiavy Chila, Dr. J.B. and the Jaguars, Wawa, and Aly Mourad.
sections.regional_variants: Salegy is part of a family of northern Malagasy musical styles including tsapiky (south), basesa (east), goma (north), kawitry (north), malesa (northwest), antosy (northwest), bahoejy (northwest), salesa (northwest), alalaosy (northwest), mgodro (Mayotte), and salegue (La Réunion).
sections.lineage: Salegy descends from the traditional antsa music of Betsimisaraka and Tsimihety peoples, itself rooted in Sub-Saharan African folk traditions. It evolved into a modern electrified style in the mid-20th century.

claims.text: Nguni stick-fighting (also known as donga, or dlala 'nduku, which literally translates as 'playing sticks') is a martial art traditionally practiced by teenage Nguni herdboys in South Africa.
Each combatant is armed with two long sticks, one of which is used for defense and the other for offense.
For up to five hours, players alternate between offense and defense to score points based on which body part is struck.
The object is for two opposing warriors to fight each other to establish which of them is the strongest or the 'Bull' (Inkunzi).

In modern times this usually occurs as part of the wedding ceremony where warriors from the bridegroom's household and area welcome warriors from the bride's household and area to meet to 'get to know each other'.
An 'induna' or War Captain / Referee from each group of warriors keeps his crew in check and keeps order between fighters.
Nelson Mandela practiced Nguni stick-fighting as a child, and it was featured on the Discovery and BBC reality TV show Last Man Standing.

sections.origins_and_history: Rebolation emerged in Brazilian rave parties in the early 2000s. It was originally called 'reboleixon'. In 2009, the name 'Free Step' was adopted by the community to distance the dance from the Axé music song 'Rebolation' by Parangolé.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The main move involves 'walking' by putting a foot forward and using the heel as a pivot point to turn the back foot backwards. The front foot turns inwards around the heel. Loose hand movements accompany the steps.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to electronic music, specifically psy trance and electro house. The music provides the high-energy pulse required for the rapid footwork.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditional attire includes bell-bottomed 'shuffle pants' or phat pants with neon details, UV reflective tape, or glitter. Modern practitioners often wear casual street clothing with flat-soled sneakers to aid in sliding.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a rave-based dance, it serves as a physical expression of electronic music. It is a social, performative style that gained global visibility through internet video sharing.
sections.notable_figures: Ralph Morente (uploader of a popular 2008 YouTube video).
sections.regional_variants: The dance is compared to the Melbourne Shuffle and Hardstyle. It shares similarities with South African 'stepping' or 'skitting'.
sections.lineage: The dance is considered a Brazilian version of the Melbourne Shuffle and Hardstyle.

sections.origins_and_history: The entrée de ballet originated in the 17th century as a component of the French courtly spectacle. It served as a modular scene within larger works like the ballet de cour and opéra-ballet. It was documented by Raoul-Auger Feuillet in his dance collections, which categorized entrances by character, number of dancers, and gender. The form largely faded from its original courtly context by the 1720s to 1790s.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The entrée is an autonomous scene where dancers enter and exit the stage. Baroque-era entrances were categorized by character style: serious, grave, comical, or grotesque. In modern classical ballet, the entrée serves as the opening section of a pas de deux or pas de trois, introducing the dancers to the audience. Specific footwork and technical execution for the historical Baroque form are not described in sources.

claims.text: An entrée de ballet is an autonomous scene of ballet de cour, divertissement, comédie-ballet, opéra-ballet, even tragédie lyrique, which brings together several dancers in and out of the scenario.
In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, baroque dance distinguished several types of entrances, according to their character and step style: serious, severe, comical or grotesque.

In his recueil de danses, Raoul Auger Feuillet qualified the entrances he described according to the number of characters and sometimes their sex: entrance alone, entrance of a woman, entrance for two, etc.
This choreographic form disappeared in the 1720s.
The entrée is the first of the five parts of the grand pas de deux and the first of the four parts of the pas de trois.
This choreographic form disappeared in the 1790s.

sections.origins_and_history: The genre originated in Spain during the 1970s, following the country's democratic transition. It was driven by a desire to modernize traditional flamenco, which had been displaced by rock-and-roll in previous decades. Key figures like José Antonio Pulpón fostered collaborations between traditional cantaores and rock musicians, leading to the definitive break with the conservatism of the Mairena era.

sections.lineage: New Flamenco is a direct descendant of traditional Spanish flamenco, influenced by the 1970s fusion movement and the subsequent urban music scene of the 1980s.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originates from the Bugis and Makassar people in Bone, South Sulawesi, Indonesia, and was historically performed in the royal palaces of Bone, Wajoq, Soppeng, and Barru.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform in a circle, moving and singing. The lead dancer, or Indo pajoge, opens and closes the performance. Key movements include 'ballung' (lying down near an audience member) and 'mappasompe' (giving gifts).
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by drums and gongs. The performance includes 20 titles of poetry, with songs such as 'Allah-Allah' and 'Ininnawa Sabbaraki'.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear 'bodo' clothes, with hair styled in a bun or 'sibollo' flower symbol. They wear a triangular crown called 'jungge' and carry a fan known as 'papi'.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically a royal court performance, it is now performed at weddings, to welcome guests, and during important government activities. It serves as a medium to bring people closer to their king.
sections.notable_figures: The 'Indo pajoge' is the lead dancer who opens and closes the show. The 'pangibing' acts as a guide for the dancers and the audience.
sections.regional_variants: Pajoge Makkunrai is performed by girls, while Pajoge Angkong is performed by transgender dancers.
sections.lineage: It is classified as an Indonesian folk dance.

sections.origins_and_history: The Grand pas was formalized in the 19th century, most notably through the work of Marius Petipa. His 1881 revival of the ballet Paquita, with music by Joseph Mazilier, established the Grand Pas Classique as a global standard for ballet companies. Other historical examples include the 2000 revival of La Fille du pharaon, which adhered to Petipa's original sequence.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance follows a specific sequence: an Entrée for the dancers to enter the stage, a Grand adage for the lead ballerina and partner, optional variations for soloists, and a final Coda. In a Grand pas classique, the focus is on classical technique without character dance or narrative progression.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is typically orchestral, composed specifically for the ballet. Notable composers associated with these suites include Tchaikovsky and Cesare Pugni. The music is structured to match the sequence of the dance, moving from the introduction to the sustained Adage and concluding with the high-tempo Coda.
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The Grand pas serves as a 'pièce de résistance' in a full-length ballet, intended to showcase the technical prowess of the performers. It is often performed independently of the full ballet.
sections.notable_figures: Marius Petipa is the primary choreographer associated with the development and standardization of the Grand pas in the 19th century.
sections.regional_variants: Variants are categorized by the number of dancers: Grand pas de deux (two dancers), Grand pas de trois (three soloists), and Grand pas de quatre (four soloists).
sections.lineage: The Grand pas is a core component of classical ballet, evolving from 19th-century court and stage traditions.

claims.text: A Grand pas, or Grand pas classique is a suite of pure dance numbers that is devoid of dramatic action.

Marius Petipa created a famous Grand pas for his 1881 revival of the ballet Paquita.
When a Grand Pas is called a Grand pas classique, it means classical technique prevails and there is no character dance.
The Grand pas is considered a pièce de résistance in the context of a full-length ballet.

sections.origins_and_history: The Jerk appeared in the United States in the early 1960s. It gained momentum through a series of hit singles in 1964, including tracks by The Larks, The Miracles, and The Contours. By the late 1960s, the dance had reached France, where it was adopted by pop artists and became a staple of the era's music scene.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The Jerk is performed individually. The dancer holds their hands at face level, crossing the wrists in front of the chest before sweeping them outward. This outward sweep occurs on the first count of the music, creating a jerky, sudden motion. The hips and legs move freely, and the dancer may snap their fingers on the first and third counts of the hand motion.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is primarily associated with 1960s rhythm and blues, though it later incorporated psychedelic music. Early tracks were typically recorded with standard band instrumentation of the era. Later, the music evolved, with artists like Pierre Henry integrating electronic elements as early as 1965.

sections.occasions_and_meaning: The Jerk was a popular social fad dance, performed in clubs and social settings during the 1960s. It is a secular dance intended for entertainment and social participation.
sections.notable_figures: The Larks, The Miracles, The Contours, Dobie Gray, Jackie Ross, James Brown, The Capitols, Serge Gainsbourg, Jacques Dutronc, Ronnie Bird, Michel Delpech, Jacqueline Taïeb, Thierry Hazard, Pierre Henry, The Go-Go's, Rocket from the Crypt, Bobby Fuller, George Harrison, Janet Jackson, The Sugarhill Gang.
sections.regional_variants: In France, the Jerk became a distinct cultural phenomenon in the late 1960s, associated with specific French pop songs and later evolving into a form of modern street dance involving detailed footwork.
sections.lineage: The Jerk is considered similar to the 'Monkey' dance, another fad dance of the 1960s.

sections.origins_and_history: The Madison was created and first danced in Columbus, Ohio, in 1957. It gained local popularity before spreading nationally in 1960 when The Buddy Deane Show in Baltimore featured it. The dance inspired teams, competitions, and many recordings during the late 1950s and early 1960s. It was introduced to Cambodia in the 1960s and remains popular there today, with large group performances such as the 4,999-participant event in Siem Reap in 2023.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The Madison is a line dance performed without partner contact, typically in lines or multiple rows. The basic step sequence includes stepping left forward, placing the right foot beside the left with a clap, stepping back on the right, moving the left foot back and across the right, then moving the left foot to the left and back across the right again. Called steps add named sequences like the Double Cross and Jackie Gleason, which dancers perform on cue. The dance is done to slow to medium tempo 4/4 music, usually between 30 and 44 beats per minute.
sections.music_and_instruments: Madison music is typically slow to medium tempo 4/4 rhythm, around 30 to 44 beats per minute. Key recordings include "Madison Time" by Ray Bryant (1959) and "The Madison" by Al Brown & The Tunetoppers (1960), which feature clear vocal calls for the dance steps. Instruments typical of these recordings include jazz piano, brass, and rhythm sections consistent with late 1950s R&B and jazz styles.
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a social novelty dance popular in the late 1950s and early 1960s, the Madison was danced on television and at social gatherings. It remains popular in Cambodia at weddings and parties, where it is performed in large groups. The dance is associated with nostalgia for the early 1960s in the US and is featured in films and musicals like Hairspray.
sections.notable_figures: Ray Bryant, jazz pianist who recorded "Madison Time" in 1959; Al Brown & The Tunetoppers, who recorded "The Madison" and other Madison-themed songs; Alan Freeman, radio presenter who recorded a version in 1962; John Waters, director who featured the dance in his 1988 film Hairspray.
sections.regional_variants: The Madison is danced mainly as a line dance in the US and France, with couple versions existing but less common. In Cambodia and the Mekong delta, it remains a popular group dance at celebrations. French versions include variations danced on disco or swing music, and multiple step versions exist.
sections.lineage: The Madison is a novelty line dance from the late 1950s US, influenced by earlier social dances like the Twist. It inspired later dances such as the Kuduro, which shares its no-contact, line dance format.

The Buddy Deane Show in Baltimore helped popularize the Madison nationally in 1960.

The basic Madison step sequence includes stepping left forward, placing right beside left with a clap, stepping back on right, moving left foot back and across right, then left foot to the left and back across right.

The Madison remains very popular in Cambodia and Mekong delta, introduced there in the 1960s.
The largest Madison dance in the world took place in Siem Reap, Cambodia, on 15 April 2023 with 4,999 participants.
In France, the Madison started to be danced in 1962, influenced by American media and films.
