sections.origins_and_history: Ramanattam was created in Kerala, India, under the patronage of Veera Kerala Varma (AD 1653–1694), known as Kottarakkara Thampuran. Its creation was catalyzed by an insult from King Manavedan, the Zamorin of Kozhikode, who in 1657 AD refused to send his Krishnattam troupe to perform at a wedding in Kottarakkara, stating the court would not understand it. Spurred by political and artistic rivalry, Kottarakkara Thampuran composed an eight-part dance drama based on the epic Ramayana in the Manipravalam literary style. Ramanattam became the immediate stem for Kathakali, which was later developed by Kottayath Thampuran at the Mridangashaileshwari temple in Muzhakkunn.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance drama is structured to be performed in eight sections, with each section enacted over a single day. The performance incorporates expressive acting, facial expressions, and movement tailored to tell the dramatic narrative of the Ramayana. The structural presentation and acting style directly inspired Kathakali. Detailed physical footwork, hand gestures, meter, and step counts are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: Ramanattam features background vocal and instrumental accompaniment designed to support the dramatic presentation of the epic text. The vocal text is composed in Manipravalam across eight daily poetic segments. Specific drum types, scales, and instrumental ensembles are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Ramanattam originated as a temple art and royal court performance in Kerala. Its visual costuming and presentation style served as the direct aesthetic basis for Kathakali. Precise garment materials, headwear, and facial paint recipes are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Ramanattam is a sacred temple art presenting the narrative of the epic Ramayana. Its eight daily plays depict key spiritual and dramatic chapters: Puthrakameshti, Seetha Swayamvaram, Vicchinnabhishekam, Kharavadham, Balivadham, Thoranayudham, Sethubandhanam, and Yudham, ending with Rama's crowning at Ayodhya.
sections.notable_figures: Key historic figures associated with Ramanattam include Veera Kerala Varma (Kottarakkara Thampuran, AD 1653–1694), who authored the plays and founded the art form; King Manavedan (Zamorin of Kozhikode), whose refusal to share Krishnattam sparked its creation; and Kottayath Thampuran, who later adapted Ramanattam into Kathakali.
sections.regional_variants: Ramanattam originated in Kottarakkara in southern Kerala and heavily influenced the development of Kathakali at the Mridangashaileshwari temple in Muzhakkunn, northern Kerala.
sections.lineage: Derived as a direct response to Krishnattam (created by Zamorin Raja of Calicut in 1657 AD), Ramanattam served as the foundational parent tradition that evolved into Kathakali under the development of Kottayath Thampuran.

sections.origins_and_history:
Stepping traces its deepest roots to the 1700s, when enslaved Africans played drums to preserve cultural traditions and communicate using percussive speech patterns across plantations. Following the 1739 Stono Rebellion in South Carolina—where twenty enslaved rebels marched down streets beating drums to rally others—colonial authorities instituted severe legal bans on slave drumming and ownership of drums to disrupt covert long-distance communication. Denied musical instruments, enslaved communities adapted by utilizing hand claps, foot stomps, and torso slaps, replacing wooden skin-drums with the human body as a percussive medium.

In the early twentieth century, historically Black fraternities and sororities adopted and transformed these body-percussion customs on college campuses. Initially centered around "Greek Sings," members gathered outdoors to sing uplifting organizational anthems. Over time, groups introduced circular walking and hand-clapping patterns to their singing routines. Fraternities pioneered aggressive synchronized choreography alongside these vocals, leading to the emergence of formal "Greek Shows" during the mid-twentieth century, culminating in the first official national Greek Show hosted at Howard University in 1976. The tradition reached mainstream broadcast television in 1992 through the syndicated series *S.T.O.M.P.*, and gained codified international reach in 2019 via the World of Step framework and the written Remo System notation.
sections.how_it_is_danced:
Stepping is primarily a ensemble percussive tradition performed by groups of three or more dancers arranged in geometric, military-style close-order drill formations. Dancers maintain a sharp, grounded posture, executing rapid foot stomps, hand claps, chest pats, and thigh slaps to produce complex polyrhythmic patterns without instrumental accompaniment. Routines seamlessly integrate synchronized footsteps, spoken-word chants, call-and-response lead vocals, gymnastics, and pop-culture choreography derived from R&B groups or children's handclap games.

Group execution relies heavily on precise spatial alignment and precise rhythmic unity. A squad leader acting in the style of a military drill sergeant frequently issues vocal commands or initiates call-and-response sequences (such as Alpha Phi Alpha's "Do it on Two"), which the line of performers answers in unison with percussive strikes. Performance tempos vary widely based on the desired beat, ranging from deliberate, heavy marching cadences to high-speed percussive sequences. Props including canes, rhythm sticks, blindfolds, or controlled fire elements are regularly integrated into advanced fraternity and sorority routines.
sections.music_and_instruments:
Stepping is fundamentally an acapella percussive performance where no external musical instruments are required. The performer's physical body serves as the primary percussion ensemble, generating dynamic contrasts through stomping shoes, hand clapping, chest popping, and leg slapping. Sound is layered through vocal arrangements including rhythmic chanting, spoken-word dialogue, singing, shouting, and high-energy organizational calls.

Musically, stepping incorporates rhythm patterns derived from African drum speech, military marching cadences, and contemporary R&B or hip-hop phrasing. Popular vocal arrangements borrow melodic lines and stage movements from legendary mid-twentieth-century Black music groups like The Temptations and The Four Tops. Each Greek-letter organization maintains an official archive of historical chants, rhythmic cadences, and signature songs performed exclusively during show finales or initiation celebrations.
sections.costume_and_setting:
Costuming in stepping reflects organizational identity, pride, and drill precision. Performers wear matching gear featuring their organization's official Greek letters and distinctive color schemes. Attire often ranges from coordinated athletic warm-up suits, custom jerseys, and boots or heavy-soled sneakers that maximize foot-stomp acoustics, to formal dress shirts and trousers accessorized with organizational canes.

Historically performed on outdoor university quadrangles, campus steps, and fraternity house plots, stepping evolved into major indoor arena events. Modern settings include college gymnasium stages, auditorium theaters, high school gymnasiums, church halls, cheerleading arenas, and international competition stages such as the World of Step platform.
sections.occasions_and_meaning:
Stepping serves as a visual and auditory declaration of organizational brotherhood, sisterhood, unit solidarity, and historical lineage. Historically used to celebrate the initiation of new members during campus probates, stepping shows allow Black Greek Letter Organizations (BGLOs) to demonstrate discipline, campus presence, and competitive spirit. While step shows are fiercely competitive contests, they foster a deep cooperative spirit across neighboring institutions through style exchanges and mutual tributes.

Beyond collegiate Greek life, stepping is widely practiced in elementary, middle, and high schools, church youth ministries, drill teams, and cheerleading squads. It operates globally as a medium of inclusive cultural expression, bridging diverse percussive traditions including Maori Haka, Zapateo Peruano, Taino dance, and Irish step dance under shared body-percussion frameworks.
sections.notable_figures:
Key pioneers in modern stepping include Frank Mercardo Valdes, who created the first nationally syndicated step contest television program *S.T.O.M.P.* in 1992 alongside producers World African Network and Vic Bulluck. Choreographers Vernon Jackson and Jimmy Hamilton of Alpha Phi Alpha's Pi Kappa chapter laid crucial technical foundations for televised step performances during this era.

Jessica 'REMO' Saul, founder of the Art of Stepping and an Omega Phi Beta sorority member, introduced the Remo System—the codified written language of step recognized by the copyright office—and created the World of Step international competition network and the first dedicated step mobile application in 2019.
sections.regional_variants:
While rooted in historically Black Greek Letter Organizations of the National Pan-Hellenic Council (NPHC), stepping developed distinct organizational style variants across different fraternities and sororities. Signature moves distinguish specific groups: Alpha Phi Alpha utilizes "The Alpha Train"; Omega Psi Phi practices high-energy acrobatic movements including "The Q Hop"; Phi Beta Sigma performs "The Nut Cracker"; Zeta Phi Beta incorporates graceful routines like "The Dove"; and Sigma Gamma Rho utilizes "The Poodle Prance".

Cross-cultural adaptation has expanded stepping into Latino Greek Letter Organizations (such as Lambda Sigma Upsilon fraternity and Omega Phi Beta sorority), where routines blend classic step percussive patterns with tropical rhythms like salsa, merengue, and bachata. Multicultural, Asian, and white Greek-letter organizations, as well as international teams across Senegal, Belgium, Peru, South Korea, Kenya, Spain, Ireland, and Italy, have established localized stepping styles.
sections.lineage: Stepping derives directly from eighteenth-century African American plantation body-percussion traditions forged after the colonial ban on slave drumming post-1739. It merges nineteenth-century close-order military drill movements, African and Caribbean percussive dance, tap dance, breakdance, gymnastics, and children's schoolyard clapping games. It has directly influenced contemporary urban dance media, drill teams, competitive cheer routines, and international percussive movement festivals.

sections.origins_and_history: Sundanese dances developed largely among common people in the mountain villages of Priangan and Banten, driven by the absence of a centralized court culture (keraton) following the fall of the Sunda Pajajaran kingdom in the late 16th century. In the 17th century, the Priangan region was held under the Javanese Mataram kingdom for 50 years, introducing Javanese cultural influences like wayang and dance styles. Aristocratic culture later flourished among the menak (nobles) in Cianjur, Bandung, Sumedang, and Ciamis, who cultivated refined arts and courtly dances.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Referred to as ngibing, Sundanese dance is typically performed between male and female couples with cheerful, dynamic, and expressive flowing movements that sync with the kendang beat. Popular styles include Jaipongan (solo, group, or couple formats), Merak (peafowl mimicry), and dances incorporating Pencak Silat martial arts movements or comical Reog routines.
sections.music_and_instruments: Accompanied primarily by the Gamelan degung music ensemble and the kendang drum. Music ranges from traditional gong degung and angklung to contemporary pop dangdut. The kacapi suling highlights aristocratic subtlety, while Rampak kendang features synchronized drumming.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed at village ceremonies, weddings, and harvest festivals like Seren Taun in mountainous Priangan rice farming villages, as well as on stages. Costumes include peafowl-inspired attire for the Merak dance and traditional regional garments.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Integrates ritual, artistic expression, entertainment, and social conduct. At weddings and village ceremonies, men dance enthusiastically to drum beats. Henry Spiller's research notes that men use dance to explore gender identities through a triangle of female entertainers, drumming, and freedom. Dances like Buyung celebrate the Seren Taun rice harvest.
sections.notable_figures: Henry Spiller (ethnographer and researcher of Sundanese dance and gender identities); traditional creators among the Priangan menak (nobles).
sections.regional_variants: Jaipongan, Topeng Sunda, Kandagan, Merak, Sisingaan, Badawang, Buyung dance, Rampak kendang, Reog Sunda, Keurseus, Badaya Sunda, Sarimpi Kasumedangan, Ratu Graeni, Dewi, and Wayang Orang in Sundanese Sandiwara style.
sections.lineage: Subclass of Indonesian dance. Influenced by Javanese Mataram kingdom culture during the 17th century and shares frames of reference with Javanese Wayang traditions.

sections.origins_and_history: Developed during the Viceroyalty of Peru with roots in the Iberian Peninsula, the dance was assimilated by enslaved and free Africans. Post-independence (1821), communities in Lima's alleyways formed cuadrillas to perform it during Corpus Christi and later Carnival. Banned by the Church in 1817 and fading mid-20th century, it was revived on stage in 1956 by Estampas de Pancho Fierro and returned to the streets in 1986 by the Movimiento Negro Francisco Congo.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced as a street comparsa led by a caporal. The choreography features dynamic pasadas de zapateo, acrobatic movements, and startling shouts to engage or frighten passersby.
sections.music_and_instruments: Driven by guitars, the cajita (a small wooden box opened and closed for rhythmic accents), and the quijada de burro (a donkey, horse, or mule jawbone hit to create a raspy buzz).
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers dress as devils, wearing horned masks, tails, and holding tridents, as depicted in 19th-century watercolors by Pancho Fierro. Set primarily in public streets, plazas, and alleys during carnivals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally associated with Corpus Christi and subsequently with Carnival and regional festival dates like San Juan in Cañete. It serves as an expression of Afro-Peruvian identity, reclaiming public space through theatricality.
sections.notable_figures: Nicomedes Santa Cruz (researcher), Pancho Fierro (19th-century watercolorist), José Durand (revivalist in the 1950s), and the Movimiento Negro Francisco Congo (returned the dance to the streets in 1986).
sections.regional_variants: Practiced historically and currently in Lima and the Cañete Province (such as San Luis de Cañete), sharing thematic traits with the broader Andean Diablada tradition while retaining distinct Afro-Peruvian instrumentation.
sections.lineage: Evolved from Spanish colonial and Catholic celebrations combined with Afro-Peruvian performance practices, drawing slight comparative parallels to the Diabladas of Oruro.

claims.text: The Son de los Diablos is an Afro-Peruvian dance that developed as a mixture of African, Spanish, and Amerindian rhythms.
Nicomedes Santa Cruz explains that, despite popular opinion, the Son de los Diablos has no links with African rituals
it was predominantly practiced by an ethnic community (in this case the Afro-Peruvian community), and it was banned from religious celebrations by the Catholic Church in 1817.
A distinguishing factor of the Son de los Diablos is its usage of such instruments as the Cajita
En 1956, el grupo Estampas de Pancho Fierro recreó éste baile como parte de sus presentaciones artísticas en escenarios.
La coreografía incluye pasadas de zapateo y movimientos acrobáticos así como gritos para asustar a los transeúntes.
Es en 1986 que el Movimiento Negro Francisco Congo rescató ésta tradición cultural y llevó la danza nuevamente a las calles.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated as a communal activity in the qasgiq (community center) for ceremonies and festivals. In the late 19th century, Christian missionaries banned the practice, labeling it 'heathen idol worship' and 'black art.' Russian Orthodox priests forbade village dance feasts as late as 1933. The tradition saw a major revival starting in 1982 at St. Mary's to ensure the survival of cultural heritage.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance follows a specific cultural format: men are typically in the front kneeling, while women stand in the back. Dancers use hand-held fans (tegumiaq) made of woven grass or wooden hoops with feathers to accentuate fluid arm movements. Rhythmic gestures are combined with storytelling and song. Styles range from 'pualla' (primarily for men) to 'ingula' (slow dances for women).
sections.music_and_instruments: The drum (cauyaq) is the only instrument used. It consists of a round bentwood frame with a handle, traditionally covered with mammal stomach lining. It is struck from above with a drum stick (cauyaun). Songs follow a specific structure: warm-up chorus, chorus, first verse, voiceless motion, second verse, and an encore (pamyua).
sections.costume_and_setting: Regalia includes the qaspeq (calico pullover), qaliq (fancy fur parka), nasqurrun (beaded headdress), and piluguuk (decorated boots). Men use wooden fans with waterfowl or owl feathers, while women use woven grass or caribou fans. Historically performed in the qasgiq, it is now performed at festivals and community centers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dance is the heart of spiritual life, used to request survival needs, tell stories, or ridicule individuals through affectionate teasing. Specific festivals include the Messenger Feast (kevgiq) and the Bladder Festival (nakaciuq). It embodies the Yup'ik conception of the world and the connection between animals and spirits.
sections.notable_figures: Shamans (angalkut) were the primary leaders and mask-carvers who mediated with the spirit world. Contemporary revival efforts were led by artists and elders in Negeqliq (St. Mary's) in 1982 to pass traditions to the youth.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include Cup'ik dance (Chevak dialect) and Cup'ig dance (Nunivak Island). It differs from Iñupiaq dance, which features standing male dancers and drums struck from below.
sections.lineage: The tradition is passed down through family lines, especially 'yurapiaq' (real dance) sequences which may be owned by individuals. It is categorized into six fundamental entities including ancestors and shamans.

sections.origins_and_history: The origins of Poomaruthan Theyyam are rooted in the migration myths of the Thiyya community in North Malabar. The deity is described as a guard of Shiva origin who resided within a blossoming flower in the form of wind. He became a 'brotherly friend' to the goddess Poomala Devi after helping her in a heavenly garden. Their history on earth begins with a voyage from a celestial realm to Malanad (Kerala) in a massive wooden ship built by Vishwakarma. Historical shrines such as those in Oriyara, Kuruvanthata, and Ramanthali claim to be the first sites where these deities were enshrined after their arrival at the Oriyara estuary and the Ezhimala coast.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is characterized by 'lively movements' that emphasize martial skill. The performer holds a sword and a wooden shield, which are the primary tools of the choreography. The movement involves 'twirling the shield and swinging the sword' in rhythmic patterns. A unique aspect of the performance is the physical contact; the Theyyam 'would knock the valyakars' and onlookers with the shield. The tempo and intensity increase as the valyakars shout to 'excite' the deity, leading to a high-energy display of ritualized combat and interaction within the temple courtyard.
sections.music_and_instruments: While the specific percussion patterns are not detailed in the sources, the performance is described as 'ritualistic dance' accompanied by 'lively movements.' In the context of North Malabar Theyyam, this typically involves the Chenda (drum) and Elathalam (cymbals) to provide the rhythmic structure for the sword and shield play. The shouting of the valyakars serves as a vocal accompaniment that drives the energy of the performance.
sections.costume_and_setting: The costume features 'special face art and body art' created from natural substances. A defining feature is the 'black mustache and beard' worn on the face. The performer wears a 'Mudi,' a large wooden crown-like ornamentation. The size of the Mudi changes according to the time of the ritual: a 'small Mudi' is used for the night Vellattam, while a 'large Mudi' is used for the daytime Theyyam. The setting is typically the 'shrine of the regional Hindu goddess Poomala bhagavathy' or associated temple grounds in Kannur and Kasaragod.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Poomaruthan Theyyam is performed during the annual festivals of Poomala shrines. It represents the protection of the goddess and the community. The act of the deity hitting onlookers with a shield is a significant ritual event, believed to be a form of divine engagement. The myth of the deity being welcomed with tender coconut water at the Oriyara temple is often commemorated during the ritual proceedings.
sections.notable_figures: The deity Poomaruthan is the central figure, described as a 'Hindu god' of Shiva origin. The Arya princess Aryapoonkani is also central to the myth, as she was possessed by Poomala and traveled with Poomaruthan on the wooden ship. The Thiyya community serves as the primary practitioners and worshippers of this tradition.
sections.regional_variants: Variants are linked to specific temple myths. In Oriyara (Kasaragod), the focus is on the welcome by Vishnumurthy. In Kuruvanthata and Ramanthali (Ezhimala), the tradition emphasizes the deity's decision to stay because of the 'beauty of the countryside.' The size and style of the Mudi (crown) may vary slightly between the Kannur and Kasaragod districts.
sections.lineage: Poomaruthan is classified as a 'Theyyam' and an 'Indian folk dance.' It belongs to the broader tradition of North Malabar Theyyam, specifically associated with the 'Shiva origin' deities and the 'Thiyya community' worship practices.

sections.origins_and_history: The Yapong dance was first performed to prepare for the 450th anniversary of the city of Jakarta in 1977. Artist Bagong Kussudiarjo organized the event after conducting months of research into Betawi life via libraries, films, and direct observation. The premiere took place at the Senayan Convention Center with 300 performers.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance features dynamic and exotic movements intended to show a happy atmosphere. It is a blend of Betawi folk dance, pop dance elements, and Sumatran dance influences. The movements were originally designed to depict the welcoming of Prince Jayakarta.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is a mixture of Betawi, Javanese, and Sundanese elements. Specific instruments used include the Rebana Biang, Rebana Hadroh, and Rebana Ketimpring. The name 'Yapong' comes from the 'ya' sounds of singers and the 'pong' sounds of the percussion.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes are based on Betawi mask dancer attire, including a headgear and a chest sash called toka-toka. The fabric often features bright red colors and dragon motifs, reflecting Chinese cultural influence in Jakarta.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally part of a ballet about Prince Jayakarta, it now depicts the association of young people. It is performed to enliven anniversaries and festive events, symbolizing joy and the welcoming of significant figures.
sections.notable_figures: Bagong Kussudiardja is the central figure, having created the dance and conducted the foundational research for its choreography and staging in 1977.
sections.regional_variants: While primarily a Betawi dance from Jakarta, it incorporates elements from Sumatran, Javanese, and Sundanese traditions.
sections.lineage: The dance is a 'new creation' that departs from traditional Betawi movements but is heavily influenced by Betawi mask dance (Tari Topeng Betawi) and Chinese-Indonesian aesthetics.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is associated with the Malacca Sultanate, specifically the era of Sultan Mahmud Shah. When the Sultan retreated to Sungai Muar, the dance was performed in the palace context for him and state dignitaries. It originated as a court dance before becoming a folk tradition in Johor.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform with 'Golden Flowers' and lit candles. It is performed by an odd number of dancers (usually 5–8) or in male-female pairs. The movements incorporate 'worship duli' (homage) and gestures of humility. The dancers must maintain balance to keep the candles lit throughout the performance.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is traditional Malay folk music, though specific instruments are not detailed in the primary source. It typically accompanies the graceful, steady tempo required for candle dancing.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers use decorations such as 'Golden Flowers' (Bunga Mas) and lit candles. The setting is usually a formal ceremony or wedding, specifically in front of the bride and groom ('King of the Day').
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a dance of royal homage, it now symbolizes happiness and well-being. It is a staple of Malay weddings in Johor, used to honor the couple and invoke a sense of prosperity through the symbolism of light.
sections.notable_figures: The community of Kampung Baru Lenga, Batu 28, in the Muar District of Johor is noted as the primary practitioners and keepers of this specific dance tradition.
sections.regional_variants: While popular across Johor, the most famous variant is localized to the Muar District, specifically Kampung Baru Lenga.
sections.lineage: Traces back to the 16th-century Malacca Sultanate court and has been preserved as a folk dance in the Johor region.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is a traditional component of Greek wedding celebrations, specifically performed in the early morning hours. Its origins are tied to the mimetic representation of a bride's physical exhaustion during the lengthy wedding rites. While the name refers to a bride, the performance has evolved as an exclusively male tradition within the wedding context.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance begins with all participants performing the Syrto Sta Dio, a basic Greek 'two-step' dance. The group moves in a line or circle. When the music shifts to a free melody, the leader separates his movement from the group to mimic fainting. He collapses to the ground while the other dancers attempt to revive him. Upon a change in the music, the leader jumps up and the entire group resumes the Syrto Sta Dio steps. This sequence is repeated two or three times.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music consists of two parts: a rhythmic section suitable for the Syrto Sta Dio and a 'free melody' section for the mimetic fainting. The transition between these two styles is the key cue for the dancers. Instruments typically include standard Greek folk wedding instruments such as the clarinet or violin, though specific regional ensembles vary.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance takes place at a wedding reception, usually in the early hours of the morning. Dancers wear the formal or semi-formal attire appropriate for wedding guests. The setting is the dance floor of the reception venue, where water may be used as a prop during the revival sequence.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It is performed exclusively at wedding receptions. The meaning is centered on the 'fainting bride' motif, serving as a humorous and theatrical acknowledgment of the exhaustion inherent in wedding celebrations. It functions as a social bonding ritual for the men involved.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance traces its lineage to the 11th-century 'Chavettu Pada' (suicide squads) of feudal Kerala, who were instrumental in the Chera-Chola wars. These soldiers were known for their rigorous training and devotion to local deities. While the martial movements are ancient, Parichamuttukali became a distinct dance form differentiated from other Kalari-based arts around the 16th century. It is primarily preserved by the Saint Thomas Syrian Christians and Latin Catholics.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers move in a circle around a central point, usually a Nilavilakku (oil lamp). They carry wooden swords and shields, clashing them together in rhythm. The footwork and body mechanics are derived from Kalarippayattu, featuring low-gravity stances and radial symmetry. The pace is variable, starting slow and escalating into acrobatic movements including flips as the music reaches a crescendo.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is primarily vocal, performed as a chorus by the dancers themselves. They are led by an Asan (chief) who often chimes bells to maintain the tempo. The songs typically begin with a tribute to God and proceed to praise Christian saints like St. George and St. Sebastian. The melodies are folk-based but contain subtle Western influences due to the history of the Christian communities in Kerala.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear a traditional white loincloth (dhoti/mundu) and red wristbands, a garb that evokes the historical attire of Kalari warriors. The setting is typically a church courtyard or a festival stage. A brass oil lamp (Nilavilakku) is placed in the center of the performance space to provide a focal point for the circular formation.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically performed as a religious offering, it is now a centerpiece of Syrian Christian entertainment. It is commonly seen at church gatherings and during the secular festival of Onam. The dance serves as a 'mock fight' (kali) rather than an actual combat (ankam), celebrating both martial prowess and religious faith.
sections.notable_figures: The central figure in any performance is the Asan, the chief or teacher who leads the singing, chimes the bells, and directs the choreography. The dance is also historically associated with the Harijan community in Kerala.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is currently most prominent in the central district of Palakkad, the southern districts of Kottayam and Ernakulam, and Malappuram in the north. While the core movements remain consistent, regional styles may vary in the specific hagiographic songs chosen for the performance.
sections.lineage: Parichamuttukali is closely related to Margam Kali, another Christian dance form of Kerala. Both share roots in the martial and social traditions of the Saint Thomas Christians and utilize similar circular formations and choral singing styles.

teaching.level_notes: Beginners focus on the basic shield-clashing rhythm; advanced dancers incorporate flips and high-speed martial lunges.

sections.origins_and_history: Dhimsa originated in the Koraput district of Odisha, India. It is deeply rooted in the culture of the tribal communities living near the Araku Valley and Borra Caves. Historically, the dance was performed by unmarried youth as a social activity. Over time, it became a universal communal dance practiced by people of all ages to find relief during working hours and to celebrate significant life events like marriages.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in a chain formation, typically consisting of 15 to 20 women who link together to form circles. The movement is dominated by synchronized footwork and hand gestures. Dancers move in patterns that create smaller and larger circles. Specific variations involve moving backward and forward with a swinging body motion. The movements are mimetic, imitating daily tasks such as farming, picking leaves, or protecting the group from wild animals.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is traditionally played by men using a specific set of tribal instruments. These include the Dappu (a drum played with a short stick), the Tudumu, the Mori (a trumpet-like reed instrument), the Kiridi, and the Jodukommulu. The rhythm of the drums dictates the pace and the 'sound of the footsteps' that gives the dance its name.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear bright, colorful sarees in earthy tones such as green, red, and yellow, typically worn at calf-length (just below the knee) to facilitate movement. They adorn themselves with traditional tribal ornaments and necklaces. The dance is usually performed outdoors, in village squares or near natural sites like the Borra Caves and Araku Valley.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dhimsa is performed for various reasons: as a relaxation during work, during matrimonial alliances, and for religious worship. It serves as a communal bond, with no discrimination regarding who can join. The 'Boda Dhimsa' variant is specifically dedicated to the worship of village gods and goddesses.
sections.notable_figures: The sources do not name specific individual dancers or choreographers, as Dhimsa is a collective tribal tradition rather than a soloist-driven form.
sections.regional_variants: There are twelve popular variations, including Bhag Dhimisa, Natikari Dhimsa, Kunda Dhimisa, Pathartola Dhimisa, Pedda Dhimisa, Sambor Nisani Dhimisa, Bayya Dhimisa, Mouli Dhimisa, Choti Dhimisa, Boda Dhimsa (ritual worship), and Goddi Beta Dimsa (forward and backward movement).
sections.lineage: Dhimsa is a tribal folk dance of the Porja and other communities in the Odisha-Andhra Pradesh border region. It has remained a living tradition within these communities, passed down through participation rather than formal schooling.

sections.origins_and_history: The Karabinye originated in Haiti immediately following the Revolution of 1804. It was named after the Carabinier rifle regiments of the Haitian army. The dance evolved from the kontradans (Haitian contredanse) and is recognized as a precursor to the Haitian méringue. It represents a hybridization of European figure dances with Kongo-derived influences such as the chica, banboula, and kalenda.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The Karabinye is a couples dance that utilizes 'figures' derived from European social dances like the quadrille and lancers. While specific step-by-step technical descriptions are not detailed in the sources, it is characterized by its evolution from a collective figure dance into a more localized partner form. It incorporates the rhythmic and physical influences of the Kongo-Haitian traditions, likely involving more fluid torso movement than its European counterparts.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music of the Karabinye is a hybrid form that accompanies the dance's transition from contredanse to méringue. While specific instrumentation is not listed in the sources, the style is defined by the blending of European melodic structures with African (specifically Kongo) rhythmic patterns including the banboula.
sections.costume_and_setting: Historically, the dance was associated with the Haitian military, specifically the Carabinier regiments. In a social context, it was performed in ballrooms and community gatherings following the 1804 independence. Specific costume details beyond the military association are not described in the sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The Karabinye served as a celebratory social dance for the newly independent Haitian population. It carries a meaning of national identity and cultural synthesis, marking the transition from colonial subjects to an independent people with their own distinct ballroom traditions.

sections.origins_and_history: Finger tutting evolved from 'tutting,' a street dance style inspired by the 2D poses of ancient Egyptian art. Its modern iteration as a finger-specific discipline gained significant momentum around 2010. Key figures like Jay 'Jsmooth' Gutierrez and Julian 'JayFunk' Daniels are credited with innovating and popularizing the style through film credits and viral commercials. The style's growth is closely tied to the rise of YouTube and digital video platforms, which allowed for the close-up viewing necessary to appreciate the intricate movements.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by articulating the fingers and thumbs to create geometric shapes, primarily squares and rectangles. It relies on 90-degree angles and the isolation of finger joints. Practitioners often use their palms as a base or 'floor' for the fingers to move across. The movement is usually performed in front of the chest or face to ensure visibility. While it can be part of a full-body routine, finger tutting is frequently performed as a standalone 'micro-dance' for the camera.
sections.music_and_instruments: Finger tutting is typically performed to hip-hop, electronic, or 'glitch' music that features sharp, percussive beats. The movements are often synchronized with 'clicks,' 'pops,' or 'snaps' in the audio track. The tempo can vary, but the style thrives on music that allows for both rapid-fire sequences and sudden, frozen poses.
sections.costume_and_setting: There is no specific traditional costume, though practitioners often wear clothing that does not obstruct the view of the hands. In some contexts, such as 'gloving,' dancers may wear LED-lit gloves to enhance the visual effect of the movements. The setting is often urban or digital, frequently filmed in close-up to capture the small-scale detail of the fingers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a form of self-expression within street dance culture, finger tutting has become a staple of digital performance art. It is used in competitive dance battles, commercial advertising, and as a cinematic shorthand for magic or technical interface manipulation. It represents a fusion of physical skill and geometric logic.
sections.notable_figures: Key practitioners include Jay 'Jsmooth' Gutierrez, who showcased the style in Step Up 3D; Julian 'JayFunk' Daniels, known for the 'Unleash Your Fingers' campaign; and John 'Pnut' Hunt, whose 'Greasy Fingers' video and appearance in Taylor Swift's 'Shake It Off' brought the style to a mass audience.
sections.regional_variants: While it is a global digital phenomenon, variants exist in how it is integrated into other styles, such as its use in K-pop choreography (e.g., Red Velvet) or its intersection with the 'gloving' community in the electronic dance music (EDM) scene.
sections.lineage: Finger tutting is a direct descendant of 'tutting' (King Tut), which itself is a branch of the 'popping' and 'funk styles' family of street dance.

basic_steps: The Box: Create a square shape using the index fingers and thumbs of both hands.
The Staircase: Stack fingers horizontally one above the other in a stepped pattern.
The Pivot: Rotate one hand 90 degrees while keeping a finger joint connected to the other hand.
Finger Isolation: Lift or fold one finger at a time while keeping the others perfectly still.

teaching.level_notes: Beginners should focus on hand flexibility and basic 90-degree boxes before attempting rapid transitions.

sections.origins_and_history: Anyeint originated as a royal court dance performed by women. Following the 1885 fall of the Konbaung dynasty, it moved into the public domain, becoming a popular hybrid of dance and comedy for the merchant class. The first troupe was formed in Mandalay around 1900 by U Chit Phwe and Ma Sein Thone.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance centers on the anyeint minthami, who performs solo and group dances to instrumental music. Comedians provide slapstick routines while the actress changes costumes. The dance is characterized by the minthami's interaction with the comedians, who provide improvised jokes and insults that the dancer must rebut.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is provided by a small all-male orchestra. The pattala (xylophone) is the primary instrument leading the ensemble. Performances include instrumental music and singing, which can be performed either with accompaniment or a cappella.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear costumes identical to those seen in traditional Burmese marionette theater. Comedians typically wear checkered-patterned Taungshay-style longyi (sarongs) and loose coats, a style innovated by U Po Sein.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Anyeint is a form of light entertainment. Historically, it served as a venue for political satire and social commentary, though modern performances are subject to strict censorship by the Myanmar Motion Picture Enterprise.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include U Chit Phwe and Ma Sein Thone (founders of the first troupe), U Po Sein (costume innovator), Zarganar (comedian), and actresses like May Than Nu and Yadana Khin.
sections.regional_variants: not described in sources
sections.lineage: Anyeint is a form of pwe (traditional Burmese entertainment) and evolved from royal court dance traditions.

claims.text: Anyeint is a traditional Burmese entertainment form that combines dance with instrumental music, song, and comedy routines.
The first known anyeint troupe was formed in Mandalay around 1900, by comedian U Chit Phwe and his wife, dancer Ma Sein Thone.
The lead singer and dancer in an anyeint performance is called the anyeint minthami.
The costumes of anyeint performers are identical to those worn by puppets in traditional marionette theater.
A small all-male music orchestra, led by the pattala (xylophone) music, accompanies the performance.
The form originated as a royal court dance performed by female dancers and was originally confined to the royal court.
Since 1988, regulations have become stricter, with comedians who perform political satire subject to arrest.

sections.origins_and_history: Bugg developed in Sweden in the mid-1940s, influenced by Lindy Hop, swing, and rock 'n' roll. Nils-Håkan Carlzon is credited as a pioneer who refined the style at the Nerikes Dance Institute. Competitive Bugg began in the mid-1970s, initially as a single 'freestyle' class, before evolving into the current social and competitive formats.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Bugg is an improvised partner dance in 4/4 time. The leader guides the follower counter-clockwise around the room. The leader uses a 1-2-3-4 step pattern, while the follower steps on every beat. Communication is maintained through arm tension and visual cues. No acrobatic moves or lifts are permitted.
sections.music_and_instruments: Bugg is danced to popular music from the swing family, including pop music from the 1960s to the present. The tempo typically ranges from 120 to 180 beats per minute (30–45 bars per minute).
sections.costume_and_setting: There is no specific traditional costume; dancers wear clothing that fits the music and 'good taste.' Shoes must be worn at all times. It is commonly danced in social dance clubs and at competitive events.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Bugg is both a social dance and a competitive sport. It is highly popular in Swedish dance clubs and at events featuring 'dansbands.' It serves as a primary social outlet for many in the Swedish dance community.
sections.notable_figures: Nils-Håkan Carlzon is identified as a pioneer of the dance.
sections.regional_variants: A variant known as 'double bugg' involves one leader and two followers. While regional dialects exist, the basic steps are consistent across Sweden.
sections.lineage: Bugg is a descendant of the swing dance family, specifically influenced by Lindy Hop and rock 'n' roll.

claims.text: Bugg is a common dance style in Sweden and is very popular on the dance floors when dansbands play.

The follower moves on every beat, placing the left foot on the 2nd and 4th beats and the right foot on the 1st and 3rd beats.
Competitive Bugg involves up to 12 couples on the floor at once to test their ability to lead and follow while avoiding collisions.

sections.origins_and_history: Swing dance originated in the 1920s within African-American communities in the United States, particularly in Harlem, New York. The Savoy Ballroom was central to this development, fostering a fusion of jazz-based movements that resulted in the Lindy Hop. Over the following decades, the dance evolved into various regional and stylistic forms, spreading across the U.S. and eventually to Europe.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Swing dances are generally performed in pairs, though solo variations exist. The technique typically involves a 'bounce' or rhythmic compression into the floor. Basic steps are often counted in six or eight-beat patterns. Partners maintain a connection that ranges from close, chest-to-chest contact (as in Balboa) to open, elastic connections (as in Lindy Hop or West Coast Swing).
sections.music_and_instruments: Swing dance is danced to swing-style jazz, characterized by a ternary rhythm (12/8 feel) that gives the music a 'bouncing' quality. Instrumentation typically includes brass sections (trumpets, trombones, saxophones) and a rhythm section (drums, bass, piano, guitar).
sections.costume_and_setting: Historically associated with dance halls and juke joints, swing is now performed in studios, clubs, and competition venues. There is no specific costume, though comfortable, durable clothing and shoes that allow for movement and sliding are standard.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Swing is a social dance, though it has developed a significant competitive culture. It is used for recreation, community building, and artistic expression. In some contexts, it is a competitive sport with standardized judging criteria.
sections.notable_figures: Frankie Manning, George Snowden, Dean Collins, and Hal Takier are key figures historically associated with the development and preservation of swing dance styles.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include the Lindy Hop (Harlem), Balboa (Southern California), Collegiate Shag (Carolinas), West Coast Swing (California), and Swing Criollo (Costa Rica).
sections.lineage: Swing dance is rooted in African-American vernacular dance traditions, influenced by jazz music, and has since branched into numerous derivatives including Jive, Boogie-Woogie, and modern competitive forms.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in the island culture of Greece. The name derives from the Greek verb 'ballizo' (to dance or jump), passing through the Latin and Italian 'ballo'. It was developed as a way for men to flirt with women in a society where direct approach was restricted.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by couples. It can be danced by a single couple with spontaneous figures, by many couples simultaneously, or in a complex form with figures reminiscent of a minuet. In Cyprus, it is specifically a men's dance.
sections.music_and_instruments: Aegean music for the Ballos is generally joyous and lyrical. In Cyprus, the music is based on the Byzantine scale and features 'amane' type songs, which are described as sad and requiring a talented singer.

claims.text: The Ballos (Greek: Μπάλος) is a Greek folk dance and a form of sirtos.
The name originates in the Italian ballo via Latin 'ballo' which derives from the Greek verb 'βαλλίζω' ballizo, 'to dance, to jump'.

This couples' dance incorporates all the elements of courtship: attraction, flirtation, display of masculine prowess and feminine virtue, pursuit, and rejection followed by eventual capture and surrender.
Its origin is in the island culture of Greece.
The simplest is one in which a single couple goes through a series of spontaneous figures.
In Cyprus the ballos is a men's dance and is interwoven with an amane type song based on the byzantine scale.
The melody of a ballos is generally joyous and lyrical which is typical of the music of the Aegean Islands.

sections.origins_and_history: The Yowlah originated as a Bedouin war dance performed after victory in tribal battles or successful pearl diving. It is a ritual of tribal unity and defense, now serving as a symbol of national heritage in the UAE and Oman.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers form two rows facing each other. Men hop from foot to foot while holding bamboo sticks, swords, or dummy rifles. They move their heads and sticks in synchronization with the rhythm. Women stand at the front, tossing their hair from side to side in the naash ritual.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes. The melody consists of seven tones in an irregular repeated pattern, accompanied by chanted poetry.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men typically wear the white dishdasha. Women wear traditional dresses. The dance is performed in open spaces during weddings, festivals, and official ceremonies.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed for weddings, national celebrations, state visits, and football matches. It signifies tribal unity, defense, solidarity, and victory.
sections.notable_figures: The lead performer is usually an inherited role responsible for training others.
sections.regional_variants: Variations include the Razfah, Ardah, al-harbiyya, and al-wahabbiyya, the latter of which is found in rural and coastal areas of Ras Al Khayma and Fujairah.
sections.lineage: Rooted in Bedouin martial traditions and tribal war rituals.

claims.text: The yowlah is a weapon dance of the United Arab Emirates and Oman, traditionally performed during weddings, celebrations, and other events.
The yowlah originated as a Bedouin war dance where men would spin rifles after victory in a battle.
The yowlah is recorded (as al-ayyala) on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage Items of Humanity in November 2014.
The largest yowlah dance as of 2019 took place in Fujairah on 26 November 2010, with 285 participants.
The yowlah is performed by men who wear a white dishdasha and hop from one foot to the other while brandishing sticks.
In the United Arab Emirates, girls wearing traditional dresses stand at the front, tossing their long hair from side to side.

sections.origins_and_history: Gnawa music emerged in Morocco from traditions of enslaved West Africans displaced through the trans-Saharan slave trade between the 11th and 17th centuries. The population originates from a broad region extending from Senegal to Chad and from Mali to Southern Nigeria, maintaining historical links with the royal Black Guard of Morocco.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The ceremony begins with an opening consecration known as the aâda, where musicians perform a swirling acrobatic dance while playing the krakeb castanets. During the lila, participants enter an ecstatic trance state called jedba, performing specialized dances corresponding to the seven families of mluk spirits.
sections.music_and_instruments: Central instruments include the hajhuj (also called guembri or sentir), a three-stringed lute played with a drop-thumb frailing technique, and the qraqab (krakeb), heavy iron castanets. Rural settings also utilize large tbel drums, while melodies emphasize the tonic and fifth with pitch-flattening around the third and seventh degrees.
sections.costume_and_setting: Urban ceremonies feature colourful, embroidered costumes, and dancers are covered by veils of seven different colours corresponding to the specific mluk spirits being invoked. Rural practices are characterized by white attire with specific accessories.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performances occur during lila or derdeba, all-night communal ceremonies of prayer, sacrifice, and healing held from late evening until sunrise. The ritual aims to reintegrate and balance the main powers of the human body through engagement with spiritual entities.
sections.notable_figures: Prominent maâlems include Mahmoud Gania ('the King'), Hamid El Kasri, H'mida Boussou, Chérif Regragui, Allal Soudani, Abdellah El Gourd, and Abdeslam Alikkane, many of whom have bridged traditional rituals with international jazz and world music collaborations.
sections.regional_variants: Maâlems often blend regional styles, such as Gharbaoui from Rabat, Marsaoui from Essaouira, and Soussi or Berber styles from southern Morocco, combining local musical flavors into their repertoire.
sections.lineage: Gnawa maintains spiritual and musical ties to West African traditions such as the Hausa halam lute, while existing as a distinct Moroccan Sufi brotherhood tradition recognized by UNESCO.

sections.origins_and_history: The tradition emerged in 15th-century Italy, where dance masters first codified steps and etiquette. Knowledge was preserved in manuscripts and later in printed manuals, with the earliest detailed instructions appearing between 1450 and 1460. These practices spread across Europe, with significant contributions from French and English sources by the late 16th century.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dances are performed either as couples or in groups (circles/lines). Technique varies by style: 'basse danse' involves feet kept low to the floor, while 'haute danse' features energetic leaps and lifts. Partners may hold each other, with some dances like the volta requiring intimate holds and lifts.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music was often composed specifically for the dance and documented alongside choreographies in manuals. Instruments and specific musical forms are not described in detail beyond the association with specific dance types like the galliard or pavane.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dances were performed in courtly settings as part of formal entertainment or social gatherings. They were often followed by hours of country dances where all present could participate. Costume details are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dance was a social activity and a marker of education and status. It was used for display and entertainment at court, but also functioned as a communal activity that could be joined by anyone present at social events.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include Italian masters Domenico da Piacenza, Guglielmo Ebreo da Pesaro, and Antonio Cornazzano. In France, Thoinot Arbeau is noted for his 1588 treatise 'Orchésographie'.
sections.regional_variants: The tradition is documented across Italy, France, and England, with specific regional preferences for dances like the branle in France or the Chiaranzana in Italy.
sections.lineage: Renaissance dance evolved from medieval dance traditions and laid the groundwork for later courtly and social dance forms in Europe.

sections.origins_and_history: In 1952, American music presenter John Coast sought to bring a Balinese dance troupe to Europe and the United States. He approached master choreographer I Ketut Marya (I Mario) of Tabanan, Bali, who had previously created the kebyar duduk dance in 1925. Working alongside Coast, dancer I Wayan Sampih, and local musicians, I Mario drew upon images of Western ballet to craft a fusion dance. The original costumes were designed by Coast's wife and tested before Western audiences in Bali. First performed by I Gusti Rasmin Raka, I Wayan Sampih, and young Raka Rasmi, the work stirred initial debate because female dancers raised their arms and exposed their armpits to represent flight. It was eventually embraced as a classic kebyar dance repertoire item.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance dramatises a garden encounter between two bumblebees. The female dancer enters first, executing complex, agile movements to depict fluttering around flowers and gathering nectar. The male dancer enters with a fan and pursues her with insistent flirtation. Though the female initially appears coy, she eventually accepts his advances. Dancers use rapid eye shifts, head tilts, and fluid torso oscillations to convey insect flight and courtship.
sections.music_and_instruments: Accompanied by gamelan gong kebyar music. Specific instrumentation detail beyond gamelan gong kebyar ensemble is not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: The female dancer wears traditional prada fabric embellished with gold paint, a long sheer scarf serving as bee wings, and a large bouquet of flowers on her head. The male dancer wears prada fabric wrapped to trail behind him like a tail, an udeng headpiece, and carries a fan throughout the performance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Oleg is a balih-balihan (secular entertainment) dance. Beyond its romantic plot, writer Kartika Suardana notes the garden symbolism conveys that both sexes naturally need each other.
sections.notable_figures: Choreographer I Ketut Marya (I Mario); presenter John Coast; original dancers I Gusti Rasmin Raka, I Wayan Sampih (1926–1954), and Raka Rasmi; ethnomusicologist Andrew McGraw.
sections.regional_variants: Originating in Tabanan, Oleg is performed throughout Bali. It is part of a broader Balinese genre of animal-inspired dances, such as the cendrawasih dance.
sections.lineage: Evolved from 1920s gamelan gong kebyar dance developments (kebyar duduk) and 1950s cross-cultural dialogue between Balinese masters and Western presenters.

claims.text: Oleg is a form of traditional Balinese dance originating from Bali that symbolizes bumblebee wildlife.
Oleg was choreographed in 1952 by I Ketut Marya (I Mario) at the request of John Coast for a tour in Europe and the United States.
I Gusti Rasmin Raka and I Wayan Sampih were the first dancers of Oleg.
I Mario worked with Coast and Sampih to draw on ballet imagery, fusing Western and Balinese dance styles.
The female dancer wears gold-painted prada fabric and a long sheer scarf for wings.
Andrew McGraw considered Oleg a classic kebyar dance in 2013.
Oleg is a balih-balihan dance created for pure entertainment.
In Balinese, oleg means swaying movement and tambulilingan means bumblebee.

sections.origins_and_history: Newa dance has developed over centuries among the Newar people, the native inhabitants of the Kathmandu Valley and surrounding regions of Nepal. The sacred ritual dance tradition known as Charya Nritya (Chachaa Pyakhan in Nepal Bhasa) possesses a documented history of more than 1,000 years. Originally, Charya Nritya was performed strictly within esoteric tantric contexts by hereditary Newar Buddhist priests known as Bajracharya as part of their private meditation practices. These ritual performances remained concealed from public view for centuries until the first public exhibition took place in Kathmandu in 1956 on the occasion of the Fourth World Buddhist Conference.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Newa dance is classified into three structural streams: traditional masked dances, folk dances, and ritual dances. Specific step-by-step footwork, posture, and technical mechanics are technique not described in sources. However, masked street dances like the Majipa Lakhey dance are characterized by vigorous movements and physical energy, with the dancer and attendants wandering through city streets. In Charya Nritya, dancers embody specific deities such as the Five Buddhas, Manjusri, Vajrayogini, and Tara, executing dance patterns that correlate with devotional chants describing the deity's form and physical accessories.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for Newa dance varies according to performance context. Masked street performances like the Majipa Lakhey dance are accompanied by loud, driving music designed for open-air processing. Songs accompanying Charya Nritya open with a ritual salutation, followed by verses that explicitly describe the appearance, attributes, and accessories of the deity being represented. Specific instrument names and tuning systems are technique not described in sources, though sacred vocal traditions have been documented in audio releases such as 'Charya: The Tantric Musical Tradition of the Kathmandu Valley'.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes in Newa dance range from elaborate ceremonial masks to deity-specific sacred attire. Masked dances utilize stylized headpieces representing demon deities, animals, and protective guardians, including the elephant mask of the Pulukisi dance and the distinct masks of the Asta Matrika, Navadurga, Sawabhakku, and Neelbarahi Naach. Performance settings include public urban streets during major calendar festivals and temple courtyards or private ritual spaces in Kathmandu, Bode, and Madhyapur Thimi.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Newa dances are anchored in both public civic calendars and private esoteric rituals. The Majipa Lakhey dance is performed during Yanya Punhi (Indra Jatra) in September by the Ranjitkar caste of Kathmandu. The Gunla Lakhey dance takes place during August, corresponding to Gunla, the tenth month of the Nepal Sambat calendar. Ritual dances like Charya Nritya function as tantric meditation exercises for Bajracharya priests, while folk forms like Jyapu Pyakhan celebrate agricultural community life.
sections.notable_figures: The preservation of Newa dance is tied to specific hereditary castes and monastic groups within Newar society. The Ranjitkars of Kathmandu are traditional custodians of the Majipa Lakhey dance, while Bajracharya priests serve as keepers of the esoteric Charya Nritya tradition. Specific individual historical choreographers or dancers are technique not described in sources.
sections.regional_variants: Regional variants exist throughout the Newar settlements of the Kathmandu Valley. Masked variants include the Neelbarahi Naach of Bode and Madhyapur Thimi, alongside the Asta Matrika, Navadurga, Sawabhakku, and Pulukisi (elephant) dances. Folk variations include Jyapu Pyakhan and Tekanpur Pyakhan. Additional ritual variations encompass Gathu Pyakhan, Kumha Pyakhan dance, and Daitya Pyakhan.
sections.lineage: The transmission of Newa dance follows hereditary and ritual lineages within Newar society. Charya Nritya was historically passed down through esoteric lineages of Bajracharya Buddhist priests. Masked dance troupes, such as those performing the Lakhey dance, are organized within localized settlement groups and caste associations like the Ranjitkars.

sections.origins_and_history: Dhemsa is an ancient tribal folk dance of the Desia, Gond, and broader Adivasi peoples in southern Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh, and the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra, India. In urban contexts, organizations like Kosodum Welfare Private Limited, Gondwana Jangom Dhemsa Rela Nrutya Dal, and Gondwana MitraMandal have organized performances of Gond Tribe artists in Mumbai to promote and preserve the tradition.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dhemsa is performed in group formations. Dancers hold each other by the shoulder and waist, executing coordinated group movements to the beat of traditional percussion and wind instruments. Specific step-by-step footwork techniques and counts are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by traditional folk instruments: the dhol drum, the tamak' drum, the changu drum, and the mahuri wind instrument. The musician playing the mahuri is known as the Mohuria, and the drummers follow the lead of the Mohuria.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occur in open tribal community spaces late at night, as well as on stage during cultural preservation events. Specific traditional costume garments are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dhemsa is generally performed late at night during annual community ceremonies including Chait Parab and Pus Puni (also referred to as Pus Parab). It serves as a major social and ritual group performance during these annual festivals.
sections.notable_figures: The sources note musical roles such as the Mohuria (the mahuri player) and cultural performance groups including the Gondwana Jangom Dhemsa Rela Nrutya Dal and artists of the Gond Tribe.
sections.regional_variants: Regional expressions of Dhemsa exist across southern Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh, and the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra state.
sections.lineage: Dhemsa is classified as an Indian tribal folk dance, often associated alongside related tribal forms such as the Rela dance.

sections.origins_and_history: Tripuri dance originated among the indigenous tribal communities living in the hills of Tripura in northeastern India, predominantly the Tripuri people who constitute over half of the tribal population, alongside the Reangs, Marmas (Mogs), and Halams. The dances historically evolved around jhum (shifting cultivation) and seasonal agrarian rituals. Over time, specific clan traditions developed, such as the Reang clan's Hojagiri dance and the Marma community's Sangrai and Owa dances. On 26 January 2018, the Sangrai dance of the Mog tribe was showcased for the first time on Rajpath during India's Republic Day parade.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance structure varies by specific tradition. The Goria dance is performed by both men and women moving village to village in a gradually increasing tempo using mudras that mimic natural movements. In the Reang clan's Hojagiri dance, teams of four to six young women balance props like bottles or earthen pitchers on their heads and lamps on their hands while moving only the lower half of the body. In the Lebang Boomani dance, men operate bamboo tokka clappers to create rhythmic beats while women wave colorful scarves to enact catching insects. Mosak sulmani uses elaborate physical gestures to mimic hunting acts.
sections.music_and_instruments: Tripuri dances are accompanied by regional indigenous musical instruments. Sowing and general folk dances like Goria use drums and flutes. Lebang Boomani incorporates bamboo clappers called tokkas alongside the flute, the khamb drum, the pung percussion instrument, and the sarinda string instrument. Songs accompany balancing forms like Hojagiri, where teams of four to six members sing while performing.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers perform in outdoor village spaces, hill slopes, places of worship, and temples. For dances like Lebang Boomani, women adorn themselves with silver chains, rings, and bangles, along with bronze ear and nose rings, while carrying colorful scarves. In Hojagiri, dancers balance props such as earthen pitchers, bottles, and lit or unlit lamps. Marma Buddhist dances such as Owa are performed in connection with visits to Buddhist temples and river sites where paper or toy boats are launched.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dances are tied to the agricultural calendar, seasonal shifts, and religious observances. Goria dance accompanies prayers during April's Garia Puja for a bountiful crop. Lebang Boomani is performed during the pre-monsoon lull; the number of lebang insects caught is believed to indicate harvest prosperity. Post-harvest dances include Mamita and the Halam community's Hai-hak dance, performed to honor the goddess Lakshmi. The Marma community's Owa dance takes place on the full moon day of Ashwin in the Bengali calendar, and Sangrai occurs during the month of April (Chaitra). Mosak sulmani serves as a hunting ritual dance.

sections.regional_variants: Variants correspond to ethnic communities within Tripura. The Tripuri group practices Goria, Lebang Boomani, Mamita, and Jhum dance. The Reang clan performs the Hojagiri balancing dance. The Halam community performs the Hai-hak dance for Lakshmi. The Marma (Mog) community practices the Sangrai dance and the Buddhist Owa dance.
sections.lineage: Tripuri dance belongs to the traditional folk and ritual dance lineages of northeastern India, originating from the jhum-cultivating tribal groups of Tripura including the Tripuri, Reang, Halam, and Marma communities.

sections.origins_and_history: The folk dances of the Sourashtra people originate within the ethno-linguistic Hindu Sourashtra community of South India. These performance traditions have developed as integral parts of religious celebrations and social gatherings. The Gebbi dance traces its symbolic identity to the concept of shakti (cosmic energy) and derives its name from Garba-graha, linking its origin to temple sanctuary worship where an illuminated clay pot or water-filled vessel serves as a temporary dwelling for deities. The Konangi jester dance derives its mythical origin from the narrative of Lord Krishna's encounter with the demon Dantavakra during battle, where Krishna used comedic dance to cause the demon to drop the Sudarshana Chakra.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The Gebbi is performed by women in counterclockwise circular formations around a sacred central point, such as a lamp (Thandili Diva) or an image of a mother goddess. If space is limited or many participants join, dancers form concentric circles moving in opposite directions. The dance incorporates circular and spiral paths with handclaps, starting slowly and gradually increasing in speed. The Dandi natana (kolane) is a stick dance performed in circular and spiral formations by tapping sticks against those of dancers on the opposite side; group sizes expand numerically from two to four, eight, sixteen, and beyond. The Konangi is a humorous jester dance performed by males using comic narrative gestures to tell stories of Lord Rama and Lord Krishna.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for the Gebbi dance consists primarily of devotional (bhakti) songs, which are rendered either by singers situated inside the dance formation or by a separate chorus standing alongside the dancers. In the Dandi natana, the primary acoustic element is generated directly by the dancers tapping wooden sticks (dandi) against those of opposing partners in rhythmic synchronization. Specific musical instruments for these dances are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: The setting for the Gebbi dance is centered around a Thandili Diva (an illuminated lamp) or a pot filled with pure water alongside statues, idols, or pictures of deities such as Amba. The Konangi dance takes place in public or temple settings during the Hindu festival of Rama Navami. Specific costumes, garments, and adornments for the dancers are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Gebbi is performed by women on various religious occasions as a worship of shakti, the primordial cosmic energy, symbolic of divine creation and cosmic order. The water-filled pot represents the outer world and acts as a sacred vessel where deities are invited to reside for blessings. Dandi natana is performed as a social and ritual stick dance during festive gatherings. The Konangi is presented during the Rama Navami festival by male performers to convey moral values and preach good thoughts to society through comical narrative theatre.

sections.origins_and_history: Nos lowen developed in Cornwall during the 1990s, emerging roughly twenty years after the general revival of Cornish dancing had taken root. It arose partly as a reaction to the more formal conventions of the earlier revival's social dance event, the troyl, which patterned itself after Scottish or Irish cèilidhs. Looking across the English Channel for alternative cultural inspiration, organizers looked to the Breton fest noz, a participatory folk model that had surged in Brittany during the 1960s. The nos lowen style was initially spearheaded by the Cornish group Sowena alongside traditional dancers, who sought to celebrate ancient regional traditions through an open, caller-free format.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Nos lowen prioritizes ease of participation, removing the caller entirely so dancers can learn directly on the floor. The style places primary emphasis on simpler and older regional choreographies, specifically highlighting snake dances and furry dances. In these configurations, dancers typically join together in winding lines or chains that move through the hall. Specific footwork counts, step names, and precise body mechanics are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: An associated progressive style of music developed around nos lowen, engineered to engage younger crowds and support continuous dancing. The music emphasizes driving rhythms and extended pieces designed to induce a communal, trance-like state that matches the repetitive nature of the dances. Specific instrumentation, tempos, and meters are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Nos lowen events take place in community spaces and dance halls across Cornwall. Specific requirements for costumes or traditional dress are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Meaning 'happy night' in the Cornish language, nos lowen serves as a celebratory social event designed to foster community cohesion and celebrate Cornish-Celtic identity. The gathering format offers an inclusive alternative to caller-dependent dances, inviting spontaneous collective movement.
sections.notable_figures: The initial nos lowen movement was spearheaded by the Cornish musical ensemble Sowena working with traditional dancers. Other prominent musical proponents who have shaped the movement's sound include Dalla, Tredanek, Davey & Dyer, and Heb Mar.
sections.regional_variants: The style is native to Cornwall. While it draws structural inspiration from the Breton fest noz, nos lowen exclusively features Cornish dances rather than importing Breton or pan-Celtic forms.
sections.lineage: Nos lowen is rooted in older Cornish dance traditions, specifically drawing on ancient forms such as the furry dance and snake dances, while adopting the event structure of the Breton fest noz of the 1960s.

sections.origins_and_history: The Shake emerged in the mid-1960s as a prominent fad dance closely associated with the British Mod subculture. Evolving out of the blue beat style, the dance surged in popularity across youth venues and nightspots, officially superseding the Twist by 1965. Unlike earlier partner dances, The Shake reflected a cultural shift toward heightened individualism on the dance floor. It became so culturally prevalent in Britain that composer Laurie Johnson capitalized on the craze with his 1965 record 'The Shake LP', which provided the basis for the central theme of the iconic television series The Avengers.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Characterized by a signature 'tense jerkiness,' The Shake involved virtually no structured steps or codified choreography. Dancers stood individually without a partner, maintaining an erratic, trembling posture through the legs while letting the head shake freely. Arms gesticulated arbitrarily to the rhythm, leaving full creative freedom to the individual dancer. A contemporary observer cited by sociologist Frances Rust described the experience of dancing to the ostinato beat as feeling 'very drunk,' highlighting the hypnotic and sensory-overloading nature of the practice.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for The Shake was defined by loud, driving rhythm and blues, typified by the electric guitar style of Chuck Berry. The musical structure relied heavily on hypnotic, repetitive ostinato beats on the electric guitar. The popularity of the beat led to commercial pop adaptations, most notably Laurie Johnson's 1965 release 'The Shake LP'.
sections.costume_and_setting: Associated firmly with the Mod subculture of 1960s Britain, The Shake was performed in youth clubs, discotheques, and music venues where loud, amplified R&B played. Mod fashion of the mid-1960s framed the dance's sharp, sudden visual aesthetic.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The Shake served as a social release mechanism for 1960s youth, exemplifying individualistic expression without the constraints of formal partner dancing. The hypnotic combination of loud music and intense somatic vibration offered a immersive experience that intrigued contemporary researchers studying the effects of music on the human central nervous system.
sections.notable_figures: While individual dancers were non-professional participants in the Mod scene, musician and composer Laurie Johnson stands out for capturing the movement's sonic marker in his 1965 album 'The Shake LP'. Sociologist Frances Rust documented the dance's physiological and social impact in contemporary research.
sections.regional_variants: Regional variants are not described in sources.
sections.lineage: The Shake evolved directly from the blue beat style within the Mod scene and displaced the Twist as the dominant British fad dance of 1965.

sections.origins_and_history: Petrunino horo originates from the Shopluk region located in middle-west Bulgaria. Over time, the traditional regional tunes accompanying the dance were documented and compiled widely in Bulgarian dance music collections. The dance transitioned from rural community settings into the stage repertoire of professional Bulgarian folk troupes, where it remains a central showcase of regional Bulgarian rhythm.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed to a 12/16 meter defined by an asymmetrical rhythmic structure: slow, quick, quick, quick, medium. This five-count pulse repeats in almost every measure of the dance. Specific footwork steps, arm positions, and line formations are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music of Petrunino horo is set in a 12/16 time signature, making it one of two key examples of Bulgarian dances in this meter. It shares similarities with the Eleno Mome tune, but differentiates itself by splitting the second slow beat into two quick counts, forming the pattern slow, quick, quick, quick, medium. Tunes for Petrunino horo appear frequently on Bulgarian folk music compilations.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes and specific performance settings are not described in sources beyond its performance by professional Bulgarian folk troupes and dance instruction environments.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Occasions and cultural meanings are not described in sources beyond its status as a core repertoire piece for professional Bulgarian folk troupes.
sections.notable_figures: Key instructors and preservers who have taught Petrunino horo include David Vinski, Dick Crum, Jaap Leegwater, and Daniela Ivanova-Nyberg.
sections.regional_variants: Regional variants are not described in sources, though the dance itself is identified specifically with the Shopluk region of middle-west Bulgaria.
sections.lineage: Petrunino horo belongs to the Shopluk regional dance tradition of middle-west Bulgaria and is closely related in meter structure to Eleno Mome.
