sections.origins_and_history: The dance originates from the Khevsureti region in the Caucasus Mountains, rooted in the martial traditions and social codes of the highland people. It reflects historical practices where disputes were settled through combat, tempered by traditional social interventions.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance follows a narrative arc: a flirting couple is interrupted by a rival, leading to a sword and shield fight involving the men and their supporters. The action is punctuated by the woman throwing her veil to force a temporary truce, with the combat resuming upon her exit.
sections.music_and_instruments: Accompanied by traditional Georgian folk instruments, including the doli (drum), panduri (lute), and other regional instruments like the chiboni (bagpipe).
sections.costume_and_setting: Men typically wear traditional chokha (men's wear) and carry swords and shields. Women wear traditional long dresses. The setting is a theatrical stage representing the mountain environment.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance serves as a performance of skill, courage, and the cultural values of the Khevsureti region, specifically the respect for women and the intensity of mountain rivalries.
sections.notable_figures: Iliko Sukhishvili and Nino Ramishvili are credited with popularizing the dance through the Georgian National Ballet.
sections.regional_variants: Related to other mountain dances like Mtiuluri and the warrior dance Parikaoba.
sections.lineage: Part of the broader tradition of Georgian folk dance, specifically the mountain-style warrior dances.

claims.text: Khevsuruli is a mountain dance that involves themes of love, courage, respect for women, toughness, competition, skill, beauty, and colorfulness.
The dance starts with a flirting couple, followed by the arrival of a second man seeking the woman's hand.
The conflict is temporarily halted by the woman's veil.
The fighting stops when the veil is thrown, but resumes once the woman leaves.
The dance is highly technical and requires significant practice.
The combatants use swords and shields.
The finale of the dance is open-ended.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance and tune emerged in the early 1850s as a variation of 'The Haymakers', a jig dating back to the 18th century. By December 1852, it became a fashionable social dance in the United Kingdom, championed by dance-masters like Eugène Coulon and featured at court balls. Sheet music was published in London and America in 1853. By the mid-1850s, it transitioned into street music, minstrel shows, and eventually a children's singing game.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced in two parallel lines of couples. Figures include balancing (Ballaneez), galloping down the inside and back, taking hands in circles with neighboring partners, and passing a partner under raised arms while the group sings the refrain 'pop goes the weasel'. In the later children's game variant, participants circle around rings and scramble for spots when the song reaches the pop refrain.
sections.music_and_instruments: Built upon a traditional jig rhythm, predominantly in 6/8 meter with an animated tempo. Historical instruments include fiddles, pianos, guitars, and mechanical street hand-organs. The music features a bouncy, repetitive structure culminating in a sudden vocal or mechanical accent on the refrain.
sections.costume_and_setting: 19th-century ballroom attire for court and private soirées, later transitioning to everyday Victorian children's and street clothing. Performed in ballrooms, stage halls, streets, and school playgrounds.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally performed at fashionable social balls, private parties, and theatrical stages, later becoming a children's playground game. The title phrase has inspired numerous interpretations, including spinner's weaver gears, tailor's tools, and Cockney rhyming slang for pawning a coat.
sections.notable_figures: Eugène Coulon introduced the fashionable dance-master choreography to court balls. James W. Porter arranged American sheet music variants. Iona and Peter Opie documented its historical folklore.
sections.regional_variants: British versions reference local London landmarks such as City Road and the Eagle pub, as well as tuppenny rice and treacle. American variations introduced alternative lyrics involving mulberry bushes, cobbler's benches, and chicken coops.
sections.lineage: Directly descended from 18th-century English jigs and country dances such as 'The Haymakers', evolving into 19th-century ballroom dances, children's singing games, and modern popular culture references.

claims.text: Pop! Goes the Weasel (Roud 5249) is a traditional old English song, a country dance, nursery rhyme, and singing game that emerged in the mid-19th century.
By December 1852, Pop Goes The Weasel was a popular social dance in the United Kingdom.
Originally, the dance was an instrumental jig except for the refrain pop goes the weasel which was sung or shouted as one pair of dancers moved under the arms of the other dancers.
Since at least the late 19th century, the nursery rhyme was used with a British children's game similar to musical chairs.
A ball held in Ipswich on 13 December 1852 ended with a country dance, entitled 'Pop Goes the Weasel', one of the most mirth inspiring dances which can well be imagined.
Eugène Coulon described Pop goes the Weasel as a very old and a very animated English dance that has lately been revived among the higher classes of society

sections.origins_and_history: Molly dancing originated in East Anglia as a tradition performed by out-of-work ploughboys during the harsh winter months. First attested in the 1820s, it became strongly tied to Boxing Day and Plough Monday, a date celebrated in the region since the fifteenth century. Unemployed farmworkers danced both to entertain themselves and to collect money during a season with little agricultural labor. In places like Brandon Creek, money raised was used to support local widows until the 1850s. Early folk collectors largely ignored the tradition, considering it unworthy of study, though collectors such as Joseph Needham, Arthur Peck, William Palmer, Russell Wortley, and Cyril Papworth recorded several dances before the original line died out by 1940.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The traditional Molly dances recorded by collectors were mostly ordinary social dances of the 19th century adapted into simple longways sets. Rather than light or intricate step patterns, dancers used heavy stepping. Dancers moved in line or set formations, often led or accompanied by character figures such as a sweeper who cleared a space with a broom. Modern revival sides, influenced by groups like the Seven Champions, have embraced a style described as more rough and wild than graceful, featuring heavy steps and sometimes complex modern choreography.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for Molly dance was typically provided by a hired musician rather than an agricultural worker. Fiddlers provided the standard accompaniment until the late nineteenth century, when concertinas and accordions became popular choices. On occasion, a musician was accompanied by a percussionist. The tunes were drawn from popular social melodies of the era, played to match the rhythm of set dances.
sections.costume_and_setting: The traditional attire of Molly dancers consisted of ordinary working clothes decorated with rosettes and bright ribbons, topped with top hats or frock coats. Dancers blackened their faces with soot as a disguise. A key feature was cross-dressing: at least one man, and in some accounts half the team, wore women's clothing. Teams were accompanied by characters such as an umbrella man to shield the musician from the elements, a broom-bearing sweeper, and a box bearer. Modern revival sides often maintain face paint, masks, ribbons, or cross-dressing while discarding standard Cotswold morris elements like handkerchiefs and leg bells.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Molly dance was tied directly to the midwinter calendar, specifically Boxing Day (26 December) and Plough Monday (the first Monday after Epiphany). It functioned as both community entertainment and economic survival, offering seasonal income for farmworkers when fields lay dormant. While pre-revival teams were strictly male, modern revival teams feature mixed-gender participation and perform both in traditional winter runs and at festivals throughout the year.
sections.notable_figures: Historical collectors Joseph Needham, Arthur Peck, William Palmer, Russell Wortley, and Cyril Papworth documented the few remaining traditional dances in Cambridgeshire villages like Girton, Histon, Comberton, and Little Downham. In 1976, folk musician Ashley Hutchings raised public awareness of the style through the compilation album Rattlebone and Ploughjack. Revival sides such as the Cambridge Morris Men, Mepal Molly Men, and the Kent-based Seven Champions played pivotal roles in establishing modern Molly dancing.
sections.regional_variants: The original tradition was concentrated in the East Anglian fenlands, particularly Cambridgeshire. Regional teams marked their village identity using colored sashes. The revival expanded the style outside its home region, spawning modern styles ranging from strict historic set reconstructions to highly choreographed, year-round performance sets.
sections.lineage: Derived from 19th-century East Anglian social dances and winter plough rituals, Molly dance is a distinct variant within the broader family of English Morris display dances. It died out around 1940 but experienced a major revival starting in 1977, growing into a recognized branch of contemporary English folk performance.

sections.origins_and_history: Arjuna Nritham, also called Mayilpeeli Thookkam, is rooted in the Bhagavathy temple traditions of south Kerala. The dance refers to the Mahabharatha legend in which Arjuna propitiates goddess Bhadrakali through a devotional performance. The art form has been preserved and transmitted through generations by men of the Ezhava community, as well as the Ashari and Kollan communities, predominantly in Kottayam and Alappuzha districts.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance movements are known as Pyattu and draw directly from the martial techniques of Kalarippayattu. Executed solo or in pairs during all-night performances, the dance is strictly tied to rhythmic songs called Kavithangal. Dancers verbally explain the specific rhythmic structure of each song to the gathered audience before physically translating those drum patterns into stepping and stance sequences.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for Arjuna Nritham centers on Kavithangal, rhythm-driven vocal compositions detailing stories from the Hindu Puranas. Musical accompaniment is provided by percussion instruments characteristic of Kerala temple arts, specifically the chenda, talachenda, and ilathalam (cymbals).
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occur in Bhagavathy temples. Dancers wear green facial makeup, ornate headgear known as Nettipattom, and a distinctive lower body garment crafted from peacock feathers (mayilppeeli) fastened around the waist in the manner of Kathakali's uduthukettu.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed as an all-night devotional ritual to propitiate goddess Bhadrakali. The costume and facial cosmetics are designed to evoke the hero Arjuna performing his act of devotion.

sections.origins_and_history: Krishnanattam was created by Manaveda (1585–1658 AD), the Zamorin Raja of Kozhikode in northern Kerala. Completed on 16 November 1653 when Manaveda was 68 years old, the dance drama is rooted in his Sanskrit text, Krishnagiti. The work draws literary inspiration from the 10th and 11th skandhas of the Bhagavata Purana, Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, the Sree Krishna Vilaasam Mahakavya, and Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri's Narayaniyam. Legend holds that King Manaveda experienced a vision of Krishna as a child beneath an Elanji tree at Guruvayur temple. Though instructed only to view and not touch the divine child, the king embraced the vision in excitement. Krishna vanished, leaving behind a single peacock feather from his headgear, which was subsequently integrated into the crown of the character Sri Krishna. The original troupe was maintained by the Zamorin until 1958, when management transferred to the Guruvayur Devaswom. Krishnanattam is historically recognized as the direct progenitor of Kathakali.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performed exclusively by men and young boys as a nocturnal temple act, Krishnanattam synthesizes the four dramatic aspects defined by Bharata Muni: movement (Angika), vocal text (Vachika), costume/makeup (Aharya), and emotional state (Satvika). Performers undergo rigorous training starting around age ten for dynamic roles (vesham) and music, or age five for chutti makeup application and playing the Madhalam drum. The movement language blends physical expression with rhythmic coordination. Footwork is punctuated by ankle bells, known as chilanka, tied over leather pads below the knees for male performers and around the ankles for female characters. Dancers navigate the performance space facing the temple lamp and sanctum, embodying gods, demons, and mortals through structured choreographic patterns.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music in Krishnanattam relies on Sanskrit slokas and padyageethams patterned after the poetic forms of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda. The vocal text is supported by traditional percussion, prominently featuring the Madhalam drum. Opening with sacred slokas such as "Jagathi sukritilokai: nandithaananthidaasa", the singers provide a continuous melodic structure that drives the physical rhythm and narrative pacing of the ensemble. Musicians train for years to sync drum rhythms precisely with the expressive steps and dramatic gestures of the dancers.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes and makeup in Krishnanattam are handcrafted by the teachers and artists. Male characters wear a starched gathered petticoat beneath a white skirt featuring horizontal orange/orange-red and black stripes near the bottom. Their upper dress consists of a long-sleeved shirt open at the back, a wooden breast-plate, chest ornaments of beads and fresh flora, upper arm bands, wrist ornaments, a girdle, and shawls fitted with mirrors at each end. Female roles wear long floor-length gathered white skirts with red borders, back-tied long-sleeved blouses, wooden breast-plates covered in red cloth, and ankle bells (chilanka). Face makeup utilizes three basic colors: pazhuppu (red-dominant orange), minukku (yellow-dominant orange), and paccha (yellow-green). A chutti—two white protruding borders along the jawline—frames paccha make-up. The most sacred garment is the headgear, which comes in two primary forms: a bun (mudi) and a crown (kiriitam) topped with peacock feathers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The performance cycle consists of eight sequential plays: Avataram, Kaliyamardanam, Rasakrida, Kamsavadham, Swayamvaram, Banayuddham, Vividavadham, and Swargarohanam, remembered by the mnemonic "a-ka-ra-ka-swa-bha-vi-swa". Each play is staged as a devotional offering with specific spiritual intentions: Avataram for the birth of a child, Kaliyamardanam to remove poison, Rasakrida for the well-being of unmarried girls and marital harmony, Kamsavadham to conquer enemies, Swayamvaram for happy matrimony, Banayuddham and Vividavadham to end poverty and ensure good harvests, and Swargarohanam for the peace of a departed soul. Because concluding with Lord Krishna's demise in Swargarohanam is deemed inauspicious, Avataram is traditionally repeated on a ninth night.
sections.notable_figures: The central historical figure of Krishnanattam is Samoothiri Manavedan Raja (1585–1658 AD), the Zamorin Raja of Kozhikode. Educated by Anayath Krishna Pisharody and Desamangalath Varrier, Manaveda authored the Poorva Bharatha Champu in 1643 before completing Krishnagiti in 1653. A statue of King Manaveda stands near the 'Panjajanyam' guest house in Guruvayur to honor his creation.
sections.regional_variants: Krishnanattam is intrinsically bound to the Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple in Thrissur district, Kerala. While the troupe has toured internationally to Europe, the United States, Singapore, and Paris, all official performances remain rooted in the lineage managed by the Guruvayur Devaswom, which employs over 70 staff members to sustain the tradition.
sections.lineage: Krishnanattam directly inspired and paved the way for Kathakali, another major classical dance-drama form of Kerala. The stylistic continuity between Krishnanattam's aharya (costume and facial makeup) and angika (bodily performance) served as the structural template for Kathakali's evolution in subsequent centuries.

sections.origins_and_history: The loyalty dance appeared soon after the Cultural Revolution started in 1966. In the late 1960s, Chairman Mao's cult of personality reached new heights, leading to citizens performing the dance to express political loyalty. By 1968, 'Three Loyalties' activities reached a climax in various areas, making the dance widespread all over the country. After the 9th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party in April 1969, the dance gradually declined in popularity, became rare by the 1970s, and rapidly disappeared as the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance consisted of a simple collective dance performed in public places like plazas, squares, or at parades. Choreographically, it did not involve much more than stretching one's arms from the heart to Mao's portrait, with basic movements originating from a folk dance popular in Xinjiang. Hand and arm movements were consistently directed toward the sky, symbolizing respect for Mao Zedong. Participation was universal and expected of miners, office workers, toddlers, and elderly women with bound feet.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance was frequently accompanied by revolutionary songs. Key songs included 'The East is Red' (东方红), 'Beloved Chairman Mao' (敬愛的毛主席), 'Golden Hill of Beijing' (北京的金山上), and 'Sailing the Seas Depends on the Helmsman' (大海航行靠舵手), alongside musical settings featuring quotations from Chairman Mao. Lyrics reinforced the political nature of the performance, emphasizing collective worship and loyalty.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances took place in everyday public settings including open plazas, public squares, and street parades. Performers wore standard daily clothing, as participation encompassed ordinary citizens from all walks of life, including industrial miners, office workers, young children, and elderly women.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance was an everyday fixture of life in the late 1960s, practiced to display lifelong devotion to Mao Zedong and exercise total discipline. It was closely linked to the ideological slogan of the 'Three Loyalties' (三忠于): loyalty to Chairman Mao, loyalty to Mao Zedong Thought, and loyalty to Chairman Mao's revolutionary line. Song lyrics performed during the dance asserted that relationship with Mao was closer than that with one's own parents.
sections.notable_figures: The central figure inspiring the dance was Chairman Mao Zedong, whose portrait served as the visual focal point for the physical gestures of the dancers.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in the Malwa area of the Punjab region. It was historically the 'Babeyan da Gidhha', performed by the elderly men of the community. It is specifically associated with the districts of Muktsar, Bathinda, Faridkot, Sangrur, Ferozpur, Mansa, and Patiala.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves performers reciting Boliaan, which are folk couplets often used for teasing. Performers must play instruments in rhythm while dancing. The technique requires the performer to know how to carry and manipulate specific instruments like the Kato and Chimta while maintaining the beat. Younger men have now joined the tradition, though the style remains rooted in the movements of the elders.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is defined by live instrumentation played by the dancers themselves. Key instruments include the Tumbi (single-string), Chimta (percussive tongs), Kato (wooden squirrel instrument), and Kartara. The Sapp (wooden clapper) is also commonly associated with the rhythm section. The music is inseparable from the Boliaan poetry.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed in the Malwa region of Punjab, the dance is typically seen in village settings and cultural festivals. While specific costume details are not exhaustive in the primary source, traditional Punjabi male attire such as the Kurta and Chadra is standard for these folk traditions.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Malwai Giddha is a social dance used for celebration and the expression of folk wit. The teasing nature of the Boliaan allows for a playful social dynamic within the community. It serves as a repository of regional Malwai dialect and oral history.
sections.notable_figures: The sources do not name specific individual historical figures, referring instead to the 'Babey' (old men) as the collective originators of the style.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is specific to the Malwa region, distinguishing it from the Majha or Doaba styles of Punjabi folk dance. It is practiced across the districts of Muktsar, Bathinda, Faridkot, Sangrur, Ferozpur, Mansa, and Patiala.
sections.lineage: Malwai Giddha is a male counterpart to the female Giddha, though it possesses a distinct instrumental and poetic character. It is a subclass of Indian folk dance.

sections.origins_and_history: Mek Mulung developed in the village of Wang Tepus in Kedah, Malaysia, establishing strong community roots by the late 18th century. It absorbed narrative, dance, and theatrical devices from regional styles including Mak Yong, Menora, and Hadrah. Originally possessing a repertoire of approximately twenty legendary stories, only a small number of these plays continue to be enacted.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances begin with the Bertabuh instrumental opening, followed by Bertabik, an opening choral song accompanied by synchronized dance movement. The physical vocabulary focuses on the upper body, featuring rapid, abbreviated arm swings that oscillate forward, backward, up, and down. Up to seven specific dances are staged across the production: Tarian Sembah, Tarian Gambang, Tarian Puteri Mabuk, Tarian Anak Menora, Tarian Sirama, Tarian Puteri Masuk Bilik Air, and Tarian Sedayung. Movement alternates with scene transitions marked by spoken dialogue and pantun poetry exchanges.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical accompaniment is predominantly percussive and driven by an orchestra of rebana drums, gongs, and kecerek (metal or wooden concussion sticks). A single small oboe provides the only melodic instrumental voice. The musicians themselves execute the singing, delivering phrases in a direct syllabic style with little ornamental inflection.
sections.costume_and_setting: Mek Mulung is performed in an open barn environment where the audience surrounds the acting troupe of fifteen to twenty people. Lead characters such as the king and princess wear traditional Malay royal attire. In historical practice, male performers wore women's dress to embody female roles; modern productions feature both male and female performers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally staged as an act of celebration and thanksgiving following a bountiful agricultural harvest, a complete Mek Mulung performance can extend across three nights. The event commences on the preceding day with a communal feast for performers, neighbors, and visitors, serving as a pillar of village fellowship and social communication.
sections.notable_figures: Pak Mulung serves as the central reciter of Hikayat texts within the performance structure. Historical productions were sustained exclusively by male actors and musicians who passed the oral repertoire directly down family lines.
sections.regional_variants: The art form is native specifically to Kedah in northwest Malaysia, with historical roots centered in the village of Wang Tepus.
sections.lineage: Historically preserved through oral transmission from elder village practitioners to their offspring, the lineage has expanded into modern institutional instruction, including academic seminars, primary and secondary school programs, university forums, and cultural preservation festivals.

sections.origins_and_history: The style was developed by Mangudi Dorairaja Iyer (1900–1980), a sanyasi and practitioner of Srividya Upasana. He drew inspiration from the devadasi traditions of the Cheyyur Sengalvarayar temple and the Melattur Bhagavata Mela. Iyer was particularly moved by a devadasi performance featuring 72 different types of items, leading him to re-establish rare forms like Suddha Nrittam, Bhattasa Natyam, and Perani Natyam within the Bharatanatyam framework.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is characterized by large-amplitude movements and a wide range of tempos. Footwork is sophisticated; dancers avoid stamping hard, instead using ankle bells to produce varied rhythmic sounds. It features extensive use of pancha nadais and gati bhedas, with rhythmic shifts occurring frequently, such as in every jati of a varnam. Body movements must be spontaneously reflected in facial expressions, requiring both physical agility and emotional introspection.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music follows the Carnatic tradition typical of Bharatanatyam but emphasizes complex rhythmic structures like pancha nadais. The salangai (ankle bells) are treated as a musical instrument in their own right, used to highlight intricate rhythms through controlled tapping rather than forceful striking. The repertoire focuses on ancient temple items rather than songs praising human kings.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear the traditional Bharatanatyam costume but with a specific addition: a special protective cotton belt worn around the waist to support the body during demanding movements. The setting is traditionally the temple or the village square of Melattur, though it is now performed on modern stages.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The style is deeply spiritual, rooted in Srividya Upasana. It rejects the glorification of human patrons, focusing exclusively on deities and rishis. The use of sringara rasa (erotic/romantic love) is common, reflecting the devadasi influence, but it is channeled toward a spiritual or devotional context rather than a neutral bhakti.
sections.notable_figures: Mangudi Dorairaja Iyer is the central figure who codified the style. He was a sanyasi whose spiritual practices dictated the themes of the repertoire. The devadasis of the Cheyyur Sengalvarayar temple are also noted as the source of the 72 types of items he sought to preserve.
sections.regional_variants: The style is a specific regional variant of Bharatanatyam originating from the village of Melattur in Tamil Nadu, India. It is distinct from other schools like Kalakshetra or Pandanallur due to its Bhagavata Mela influences and specific rhythmic techniques.
sections.lineage: The lineage flows from the temple devadasi traditions and the Melattur Bhagavata Mela through Mangudi Dorairaja Iyer to his students. It shares roots with Kuchipudi, particularly in the execution of Suddha Nrittam and the use of the clay pot in Perani Natyam.

sections.origins_and_history: Kummattikali is a traditional folk dance rooted in the Malabar region of Kerala, specifically within the Thrissur and Palakkad districts. It is categorized as a devotional ritual art form, often linked to Shaiva mythology. The 'pristine' or original version of the dance is historically associated with the Bhadrakali temple in Palakkad. Over generations, it has become an inseparable part of the Onam festival celebrations, where it serves as both a religious offering and a form of communal entertainment.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves performers moving in a procession from house to house. The movement is characterized by the manipulation of long agricultural sticks called Kummattikali. The troupe is led by a character named Thamma, who portrays an old woman walking with a stick. While specific footwork patterns are not detailed in the primary sources, the dance is rhythmic and coordinated with the vibrations of the Onavillu instrument. Performers interact with the public, collecting gifts while enacting scenes from mythology.
sections.music_and_instruments: The primary musical accompaniment is the Onavillu, a bow-like instrument made from areca nut wood. The sound is produced by beating the strings of the bow with a narrow bamboo stick, creating a vibrating rhythmic foundation. The songs accompanying the dance include folk tales like Manjan Nayare Pattu and episodes from the Ramayana and Shiva myths.
sections.costume_and_setting: The costume is the most distinctive element, featuring masks carved from woods like jackfruit, Hog Plum, or Coral tree. These masks depict characters like Krishna, Narada, or hunters, often featuring a 'talla' (toothless mouth). The dancers' bodies are covered in skirts of plaited grass or bunches of grass to create a bushy appearance. The setting is typically the outdoors, moving through village streets and residential courtyards during the Onam festival.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Kummattikali is performed during the Onam festival. It is a devotional act intended to please deities, classified as a ritualistic art form. The character of Thamma represents the mother of all beings, lending a spiritual depth to the performance. The act of moving from house to house to collect rice and jaggery reinforces communal bonds and celebrates the harvest season.
sections.notable_figures: The sources do not name individual historical dancers, but they highlight specific mythological figures portrayed: Krishna, Narada, Kiratha, Darika, and the central character Thamma (the old woman).
sections.regional_variants: The dance is prevalent in Thrissur and Palakkad districts. The Palakkad variant, specifically at the Bhadrakali temple, is noted as the 'pristine' or original form of the tradition.
sections.lineage: Kummattikali belongs to the devotional category of Kerala's ritualistic folk arts. It shares a cultural landscape with other ritual forms like Theyyam, Thirra, and Poothamthira, though it is distinct in its use of grass costumes and the Onavillu instrument.

sections.origins_and_history: The tradition originated in the Johor–Riau and Riau–Lingga sultanates, circulating through dynastic marriages and trade networks. It was introduced to Pahang in 1811 for a royal wedding and later moved to Terengganu in 1915. The most significant development occurred under Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah (1920–1942) and Tengku Ampuan Mariam, who formalised the repertoire. After a post-WWII decline, it was revived in the 1960s.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance, historically called Joget Gamelan, features female dancers known as budak joget. It is characterized by highly stylized, refined movements including specific hand gestures and controlled footwork. Performances were historically held in palace settings and could last from evening until dawn. The technique emphasizes grace and courtly decorum, with choreography often involving props like fans or scarves in pieces such as Topeng.
sections.music_and_instruments: The ensemble is smaller than Javanese gamelan and consists of metallophones, gongs, drums, and xylophones. Specific instruments include the keromong (bonang), gambang (xylophone), demung, saron, kenong, and gongs. The music is percussion-based and provides a rhythmic and melodic framework for the dance, with some melodies, like Timang Burung, showing possible influences from Chinese folk music.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear elaborate court costumes and headdresses. Historical accounts by Frank Swettenham describe the setting as ceremonial palace halls. The attire was distinct to the Pahang and Terengganu courts, featuring variations in headdress styles that distinguished the repertoire from other regional dance traditions.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically, Malay gamelan was a private court entertainment performed for royal weddings, receptions, and installations. It served as a symbol of aristocratic prestige and ceremonial refinement. Today, it functions as a public performing art and a symbol of Malaysian intangible cultural heritage, performed at cultural festivals and institutional events.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include Sultan Ahmad Al-Mu’adzam Shah of Pahang, his consort Che Zubedah, and their daughter Tengku Ampuan Mariam. Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah of Terengganu was a major patron. Encik Basuk was a notable musician from Lingga who helped train performers in Pahang during the 19th century.
sections.regional_variants: Historically known as Gamelan Pahang or Joget Pahang when centered in Pekan. After moving to Terengganu, it became known as Joget Terengganu or Gamelan Terengganu. While related to Javanese and Balinese traditions, it is distinct in its smaller ensemble size and specific Malay court repertoire.
sections.lineage: It is a subclass of the wider Southeast Asian gamelan family and Malay classical music. It is directly descended from the court traditions of Johor-Riau and Riau-Lingga, with specific developments occurring in the Pahang and Terengganu royal lines.

sections.origins_and_history: Originating in Veracruz, Mexico, the dance is linked to the Old Germanic word 'raspere'. It gained significant popularity as a social dance after 1945 in Mexico and Cuba. Some theories suggest it may be a descendant of European 'Strohschneider' jumping dances seen in 16th-century paintings by Pieter Bruegel.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance features a 'scraping' movement where dancers jump and thrust one heel forward, then quickly switch to the other. This is typically performed in a 6/8 meter. Partners often link elbows or hold hands to swing around during the melodic chorus sections between the scraping steps.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is defined by a 6/8 time signature and the use of the Güiro, a scraper instrument that produces a ratchet-like sound. It is often performed by folk ensembles and is a key component of the 'Mexican Hat Dance' medley.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed in festive settings such as schools and celebrations. Dancers typically wear traditional Mexican folk attire, such as colorful ruffled skirts for women and charro-influenced clothing for men.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: La Raspa is a celebratory dance used for social gatherings. It is also a foundational piece for dance education in schools. Historically, it has been associated with harvest or fertility themes in its ancestral forms.
sections.notable_figures: Specific individual creators are not named in sources, but the dance was popularized internationally after 1950, spreading through social dance circles in Europe.
sections.regional_variants: Variants exist in Mexico and Cuba. It is frequently combined with the Jarabe Tapatío in modern performances.
sections.lineage: Subclass of Mexican folk dance; potentially influenced by or related to the European 'Wechselhupftanz' (alternating jump dance) tradition.

sections.origins_and_history: Lezim originated in the rural villages of Maharashtra and Gujarat as a form of physical conditioning and martial practice. Historically, it involved heavier implements like the Reedh (a 2.5-foot bamboo pole with iron chains) or the Koyande (a weighted wooden pole), which were used for strength training. Over time, these evolved into the lighter musical instruments used today. The dance gained significant institutional recognition when it was incorporated into school fitness regimes and military drills, eventually being showcased internationally at the 1982 Asian Games.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by a minimum of 20 dancers, usually in two rows, four rows, or concentric circles. Dancers follow a sequence of steps that change every few beats, often totaling 25 different movements in a short performance. The 'ring leader' uses a whistle to announce changes in the choreography. Movements include twirling, stepping in unison, and striking the Lezim instrument to create a jingling sound. It is characterized by vigorous calisthenic moves and physical feats performed to the rhythm of drums.
sections.music_and_instruments: The central instrument is the Lezim, a wooden pole (todanna bandhaleli) with a chain (adakavalelya) and metal discs. Percussion is provided by the dholki (a narrow drum) and the halagi. Large cymbals (talasarakhe) with wide mouths are also used. The music is primarily rhythmic and instrumental, designed to drive the high-tempo movements of the dancers.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear vibrant, colorful costumes typical of Maharashtrian folk traditions. The dance is performed outdoors in various settings, including school grounds for fitness drills, village streets during Jatras (religious processions), and public squares during the Ganesh festival.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Lezim is performed during the Ganesh festival (Ganeshotsav) and village Jatras. It serves as a communal celebration and a display of physical fitness. In educational and military contexts, it is used as a discipline-building exercise and a rhythmic drill.
sections.notable_figures: While individual dancers are rarely named in folk traditions, the 400 Maharashtrian players who performed at the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi are cited as a significant collective that brought the dance to international attention.
sections.regional_variants: Three main types exist: military lezim (martial art focus, popular in Baroda), talathekya, and samanyajananna. Historical variations included the use of the 2.5-foot Reedh bamboo pole and the 18-inch Koyande wooden pole with heavy iron chains.
sections.lineage: Lezim is classified as an Indian folk dance and a 'game and martial dance.' It shares formation characteristics with the Garba of Gujarat, particularly in its concentric circle variants (samuhanrtyanta nartakam).

sections.origins_and_history: M'alayah originates in the northern regions of Oman and the northeastern United Arab Emirates. It is a traditional Arab folk dance that has historically been performed at weddings and social gatherings. The dance is also noted for its presence in East Africa, indicating a shared cultural history through trade routes. It is considered by some to be a precursor to modern belly dancing.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is defined by rapid, rhythmic movements of the hips and buttocks. Dancers synchronize these isolations with the beat of local folk songs. The technique involves high-frequency vibrations of the lower body, often maintaining a stable upper body to emphasize the pelvic and gluteal motion. Specific footwork and arm positions are not detailed in the primary sources, but the focus remains on the intensity of the hip movements.
sections.music_and_instruments: M'alayah is performed to local popular folk songs. The music is typically percussive and rhythmic to support the rapid movements of the dancer. While specific instruments are not named in the sources, the genre is categorized under Arab folk music, which traditionally utilizes drums and vocal accompaniment common to the Gulf region.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is most commonly performed at weddings. Dancers typically wear traditional Gulf attire, though the sources do not specify unique costume requirements beyond the standard celebratory dress of the region. The setting is usually a social, communal space such as a wedding hall or a private home during festivities.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: M'alayah is a celebratory art form. Its primary function is to provide entertainment and express joy during significant life events, particularly weddings. It serves as a medium for social bonding and the preservation of regional folk identity.
sections.notable_figures: not described in sources
sections.regional_variants: The dance exists in both Eastern Arabia (Oman and UAE) and East Africa. While the core movement of hip vibration remains consistent, the specific folk songs and social contexts may vary between these two major regions.
sections.lineage: M'alayah is classified as a Middle Eastern and Arab folk dance. It is linked to the broader family of belly dance and shares stylistic similarities with African dances like Makossa and Mapouka.

sections.origins_and_history: Mujra emerged during Mughal rule in the Indian subcontinent as a performance for the elite class and nawabs. It was traditionally a family art passed from mother to daughter in cultural centers like Delhi, Lucknow, and Lahore. Tawaifs, or courtesans, were the primary practitioners and were often considered authorities on etiquette and culture, sometimes likened to Japanese geishas.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance combines elements of classical Kathak with sophisticated gestures. It is described as elegant and artistic, often involving the dancer being the center of public eye for long periods. The term 'mujra' itself refers to a deferential salute or payment of respects, which is reflected in the opening and closing movements of the performance.
sections.music_and_instruments: The performance is set to Hindustani classical music, specifically genres like thumri and ghazal. It incorporates poetry from the Mughal period, including works from the reigns of Akbar to Bahadur Shah Zafar. The music provides a medium for exchange between the solo female dancer and her audience.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditionally performed in mehfils (intimate gatherings) or kothas (special houses/salons). In historical contexts like Lahore's Heera Mandi, these settings were hubs for musicians and dancers. Costumes are typically artistic and feminine, designed to make the dancer appear fluent and elegant.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically, tawaifs were invited to perform at significant events such as marriages or the birth of a male heir. The dance signifies a 'payment of respects' or a 'deferential salute.' In the modern era, it is performed at weddings, birthdays, and bachelor parties.
sections.notable_figures: The sources mention tawaifs as a class of performers who were authorities on culture. In cinema, the dance is associated with characters like Umrao Jaan. Modern documentary subjects include the performers featured in 'Showgirls of Pakistan' (2021).
sections.regional_variants: The performers are known by different names across the subcontinent: tawaifs in North India and Pakistan, baijis in Bengal, and naikins in Goa. Lahore's Heera Mandi and Mumbai's Congress House are noted as specific regional hubs.
sections.lineage: Mujra is a subclass of Asian dance and a derivative of the classical Kathak tradition. It has influenced and been influenced by the 'Nautch' tradition and modern South Asian film choreography (Bollywood/Lollywood).

sections.origins_and_history: Chandor, originally Chandrapur, was the capital of the Kadamba dynasty. The dance is linked to King Harihara I of the Vijayanagara Empire, who reportedly performed it in 1390 after defeating a Chola ruler. It also commemorates the fall of the Yadav dynasty.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers form two rows and march to a specific beat, later forming a circle to simulate grain pounding with pestles. A lead dancer holds a leash attached to a participant in a bear costume. The routine includes a symbolic sweeping of the ground by a Devadasi girl.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is provided by the ghumot, kansaalle (jhanjh), and dholke. The pestles themselves are instruments, containing internal bells or blades. Songs are strictly oral and contain historical hymns.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear a dhoti, long-sleeved shirt, black jacket, and a turban (pagdi). The dance occurs in front of the village church and in the yards of local houses, accompanied by torchbearers called divtekars.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a Shigmo tradition, it is now performed on the second day of the Goa Carnival. It serves as an artistic commemoration of historical victories and the Kadamba period.
sections.notable_figures: King Harihara I of the Vijayanagara Empire is cited as a historical performer of the dance in 1390.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is specifically preserved in the village of Chandor in the Salcete region of Goa.
sections.lineage: The dance claims lineage from the Satavahana and Kadamba dynasties, with influences from the Vijayanagara Empire.

sections.origins_and_history: Marathukali is a specialized variant of Poorakkali, a ritual dance performed during the Pooram festival in North Malabar. The dance is based on the Vasanthapooja, a worship ritual performed by inhabitants of different worlds to honor Kamadeva. Originally, the myth suggests women and heavenly goddesses like Rambha performed these rites to celebrate the reincarnation of the god of love after he was burned by Shiva. Over time, men from specific sects including the Thiyya, Maniyani, and Nambiar took charge of the festivities, though young girls still maintain a role in the broader ritual context. The survival of the form is credited to the Panickers, who have served as the traditional masters and expanders of the art.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by a troop of young men moving around a central lit lamp called a nilavilukku. The technique is characterized by masculine movements and acrobatic steps influenced by martial arts. Dancers do not use external instruments; instead, they maintain rhythm through synchronized foot-thumping and clapping. The formation is typically a circle around the lamp. The performance is physically demanding, requiring a month of strenuous practice and abstinence. The leader, or Panicker, initiates the songs which the dancers repeat in chorus while executing their movements.
sections.music_and_instruments: There are no external singers or musical instruments used in Marathukali. The music is entirely vocal and percussive, generated by the dancers themselves. The repertoire consists of hymns and songs drawn from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Bhagavata. The Panicker leads the singing, and the dancers provide a rhythmic backing through hand claps and heavy, synchronized footwork that serves as the primary percussive element.
sections.costume_and_setting: The performance takes place in the precincts of Bhagavathy temples in North Malabar, specifically around a multi-tiered oil lamp (nilavilukku). The dancers are described as being 'decked in lion costumes' in certain contexts of the ritual, emphasizing the masculine and powerful nature of the performance. The setting is nocturnal, illuminated by the central lamp during the nine days of the Pooram festival.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Marathukali is performed during the nine-day Pooram Thiyya festival, starting with the Karthika asterism and ending with the Pooram asterism in the month of Meenam (March-April). It is a ritual of 'Vasanthapooja' intended to spread knowledge and provide entertainment. While the standard Poorakkali is a devotional act, the Marathukali variant is a competitive event where two parties engage in disputes, testing their knowledge of scriptures and their physical skill.
sections.notable_figures: The Panickers are the most significant figures in the tradition, acting as leaders, scholars, and instructors. They are credited with the survival and expansion of Poorakkali and Marathukali through generations.
sections.regional_variants: Marathukali itself is a variant of Poorakkali. The primary difference lies in the 'competent mood' of Marathukali, where two parties compete against each other, leading to scholarly disputes, whereas the ordinary Poorakkali lacks this competitive element.
sections.lineage: The dance is passed down through the Thiyya, Maniyani, and Nambiar communities of Kerala. It is supported by the Kerala Folklore Academy and remains a vital part of the cultural identity of North Malabar.

sections.origins_and_history: Kuthiyottam is rooted in the ancient traditions of Kerala, specifically associated with the worship of the warrior goddess Bhadrakali. Scholars have theorized that the ritual evolved from 'mock human sacrifice' practices that existed in the region's early history. The dance serves as a living reenactment of the goddess's mythological battles, where the young performers represent her loyal, battle-worn soldiers. It is traditionally performed during the Pongala festival in the month of Kumbham.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is characterized by highly energetic, synchronized movements performed by a group of boys. Under the direction of an asan (conductor), the performers execute steps that are paced to the rapid beat of traditional drums. The boys act as both dancers and singers, chanting rhythmic verses while moving. The technique requires high stamina and precision to maintain synchronization during the intense, fast-paced sequences that mirror the chaos and triumph of battle.
sections.music_and_instruments: The primary musical accompaniment is provided by traditional Kerala drums, which dictate the tempo and energy of the performance. The dancers themselves provide the vocal component, singing songs that are synchronized with the legends of the goddess. The music is rhythmic and driving, designed to sustain the high-energy physical output of the young performers throughout the ritual procession.
sections.costume_and_setting: During the preparation phase, boys wear simple ascetic clothes. For the final performance, they change into elaborate ceremonial costumes. This often includes traditional headgear, waistbands, and ornaments. The setting is typically a Hindu temple dedicated to Bhadrakali or Durga, or the processional routes leading to these temples during the annual Pongala festival celebrations.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The ritual takes place during the annual Pongala festivals. It is a form of spiritual offering where the physical suffering and discipline of the boys are seen as a sacrifice to the goddess. The piercing and subsequent blood are symbolic of the wounds sustained by the goddess's army. It is believed to bring protection and favor to the community and the families of the volunteers.
sections.notable_figures: The 'asan' is the central figure in Kuthiyottam, serving as the conductor, teacher, and spiritual guide for the young boys. The asan is responsible for training the volunteers in the songs, steps, and the strict ascetic codes required for the ritual.
sections.regional_variants: Variants of the dance and its associated piercing rituals are found in the Bhadrakali temples of the Alappuzha, Kollam, and Thiruvananthapuram districts. While the core elements of asceticism and rhythmic dance remain constant, the intensity of the piercing and the specific choreography may vary between different temple troupes.
sections.lineage: The dance is passed down through temple-affiliated troupes and families. It is a communal tradition where the role of the asan is often hereditary or earned through years of dedicated practice within the specific ritual framework of a temple.

sections.origins_and_history: The Matki Dance originated in the Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh, India. It developed as a folk expression among the women of the region, used to celebrate domestic and communal milestones. The dance is named after the 'matki', the Hindi term for a small earthenware pitcher, which has been a staple of Indian household life for centuries. It remains a living tradition, passed down through oral and physical instruction within families.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is a solo performance where a woman balances an earthen pot on her head while moving in a circular pattern. The dancer often covers her face with a veil, requiring significant spatial awareness and balance. The movement is coordinated with the beats of the dhol. Two specific subtypes of the dance exist: Aada Nach and Khada Nach, which represent variations in the style and rhythm of the performance.
sections.music_and_instruments: The primary musical accompaniment is the dhol, a traditional double-headed drum. The dhol provides the rhythmic foundation that dictates the dancer's steps and the overall tempo of the performance. No other specific instruments are cited as central to the tradition in the primary records, though the rhythmic clapping of the surrounding circle often accompanies the drum.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear traditional Indian attire, specifically sarees or lehengas, which are richly decorated with ornaments. A key feature of the costume is the veil (ghunghat) used to cover the face during the performance. The setting is typically an outdoor or communal indoor space during festive occasions like weddings or birthdays, where spectators form a circle around the solo performer.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Matki Dance is performed on special occasions that mark significant life events, such as weddings and the birth of a child. It serves as a celebratory ritual, showcasing the dancer's skill, grace, and ability to maintain composure under the weight of the symbolic household pitcher. It is a secular folk dance, though it carries the weight of regional identity.

sections.regional_variants: The dance is specific to the Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh. Within this tradition, the subtypes Aada Nach and Khada Nach are recognized as distinct variations of the movement and rhythm.

sections.origins_and_history: The Pandanallur style developed primarily in the village of Pandanallur within the Thanjavur district of Tamil Nadu. Its foundation stems from the Thanjavur Quartet—four brothers who served as court composers in the early 19th century. Meenakshisundaram Pillai, a descendant of these nattuvanars, shaped the style into its definitive modern form during his lifetime from 1869 to 1964.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced through rigorous adavu techniques emphasizing linear geometry. Hard floor stamping is replaced by controlled slow movements that maximize the acoustic output of the salangai ankle bells. Every step is distinctly marked with exactness and accuracy to achieve rhythmic vitality.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music features traditional classical repertoire including Tanjore Quartet pada-varnams and jatiswarams composed in specific ragas such as Vasantha, Saveri, Chakravakam, Kalyani, and Bhairavi. Acoustic accompaniment centers on rhythmic footwork interacting with salangai ankle bells.
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally performed in classical settings, court contexts, and modern proscenium stages, conveying dramatic storytelling through understated abhinaya and abstract rhythmic passages.

sections.origins_and_history: The Raut are an Indian caste whose traditional occupation is to rule and herd cattle, with historical ties suggesting they may have been a tribal militia in Chhota Nagpur originating from the Kawar. In the 20th century, the community underwent Sanskritisation, adopting the customs and values of high-caste Hindus.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performed on Diwali, the Rauts sing and dance in a group with sticks in their hands in the village pathways. Detailed footwork, rhythm, and body movement techniques are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance involves group singing, and Raut men traditionally performed the local folk epic Candaini in a combination of dance and song. Specific musical instruments are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: During the dance, the Rauts wear a special costume. The performance takes place outdoors in the village pathways.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Raut Nacha is performed on Diwali. Traditionally, the Raut community's main business and occupation involved herding and milking cattle and selling milk products.
sections.notable_figures: Not described in sources, though the Candaini epic features the characters princess Chanda and Veer Lorik.
sections.regional_variants: The Rauts are mainly found in Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, and Maharashtra, specifically in districts like Durg, Raipur, Bastar, Nagpur, and Bhandara. Sub-castes include Gawala, Thetwar, Jheriya, and Kosariya.
sections.lineage: The dance is linked to the Raut caste and the performance of the Candaini folk epic originating within the community.

sections.origins_and_history: Introduced in the 18th century by Kunchan Nambiar, Ottan thullal was born from a desire to critique society through satire. It is influenced by the Natya Shastra and has historical ties to the Ambalapuzha temple complex, where it was once banned due to its biting social commentary.

sections.costume_and_setting: The performer wears green makeup and a colorful costume decorated with a long red and white band and painted wooden ornaments.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The art form is used for social criticism and satire, often parodying landlords, prominent citizens, and human prejudices. It is also used in competitions and to spread social messages.
sections.notable_figures: Kunchan Nambiar (founder), Mathur Panikkar (popularizer).
sections.regional_variants: Seethankan thullal and Parayan thullal are closely related art forms.

sections.origins_and_history: Leventikos is a traditional dance rooted in western Macedonia, practiced by Slav Macedonians and Greeks across Florina, Resen, and Bitola. It shares historical musical ties with Balkan ballads and regional dance forms.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance steps follow a slow-quick-quick-slow-quick pattern corresponding to a five-beat meter. The style performed in Petroussa differs significantly from the version in Florina. Other technical details like precise posture and arms are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is built on asymmetric meters of 12/8 (3+2+2+3+2) and 16/8 (4+2+3+4+3). Tunes like Ibraim Odza are performed in multiple metric variations, sharing rhythmic space with dances like Pušteno and Beranče.
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed in community contexts across western Macedonia, the Buvčansko theme has also entered popular culture through its inclusion in Civilization VI.

sections.lineage: Classified as a subclass of the hora dance family, sharing metric structures with regional tunes like Berace, Beranče, Bajrače, and Pušteno.

sections.origins_and_history: The ballo emerged during the Italian Quattrocento as a sophisticated Renaissance dance form. Fifteenth-century dance masters Domenico da Piacenza and Guglielmo Ebreo da Pesaro composed numerous balli and authored foundational treatises containing choreography and theoretical principles. By the Baroque period, the form expanded significantly, incorporating vocal numbers in works by Claudio Monteverdi and Francesco Lambardi, and instrumental interludes by composers such as George Frideric Handel.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers move with a debita misura, maintaining a gentle, moderate, and sweet manner. The body is held with a noble and lordly carriage, remaining light on the feet with well-formed gestures. Dancers keep their gaze cast modestly toward the ground with the head held straight. At the end of the dance, participants perform reciprocal, pious reverences toward their partners before retiring with a modest attitude.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for the fifteenth-century ballo was structured around four distinct misure: the slow bassadanza, the quadernaria (one-sixth faster), the saltarello (two-sixths faster), and the piva (twice as fast). Later Baroque iterations incorporated lute tablatures, soprano voice scores, two recorders, and violins as seen in Handel's revisions of Il pastor fido.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance was performed in Renaissance noble courts, chambers, and civic festival spaces. Participants wore formal court attire appropriate to the Quattrocento and subsequent Baroque periods, reflecting their high social standing and the elite nature of the gatherings.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Considered a vital branch of gymnastics and a study in personal elegance, the ballo was designed to bestow a gracious presence, fine posture, and smooth gait while banishing clumsiness. It was practiced during civic celebrations, courtly festivities, and elite social gatherings, though masters cautioned against the moral hazards of human vanity in such settings.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical figures include Domenico da Piacenza, Guglielmo Ebreo da Pesaro, Fabritio Caroso da Sermoneta, Claudio Monteverdi, Francesco Lambardi, Giambattista Dufort, and George Frideric Handel.
sections.regional_variants: Treatises distinguish between Italian, French, and Spanish styles of balli and balletti, noting shifts in foot positions and stylistic preferences across European courts, particularly as French theatrical dance gained prominence in the early eighteenth century.
sections.lineage: The ballo shares lineage with the medieval basse danse and influenced later theatrical ballet, the tarantella, and various Baroque balletti forms.

movement_profile.footwork: Light on the feet (leggiera in sul piede) with smooth and measured walking steps.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Well-formed gestures (giesti bene formati) accompanying modest and controlled body movement.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Controlled, humble, and meek body movement (umile e mansueto) reflecting personal grace.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Walking in columns or lines (in schiera) within noble chambers or performance spaces.
movement_profile.partnering: Partners interact with graceful turns, leading and following, concluding with a mutual, respectful reverence.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Shifting dynamically between slow, measured pacing and accelerated ratios (one-sixth, two-sixths, and double speed).

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Grounded footwork with light stepping; origins of the name connect to jumping about (ballizō), but 15th-century court treatises emphasize measured lightness.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid wandering eyes, tossing the head high, carrying the chin down in the chest, awkwardness (goffaggine), and unseemly vanity.

sections.origins_and_history: Calypso music has its roots in Trinidad in the 17th century from the West African Kaiso and Canboulay familiar to the enslaved Africans brought to the Caribbean islands to work on sugar plantations. Modern calypso began in the 19th century as a fusion of disparate elements ranging from the masquerade song lavway, French Creole belair, and the calinda stick-fighting chantwell. Its early rise was closely connected with the adoption of Carnival by Trinidadian slaves, growing significantly after the abolition of slavery in 1834.
sections.how_it_is_danced: not described in sources
sections.music_and_instruments: Calypso music is characterized by highly rhythmic and harmonic vocals, traditionally accompanied by steel drums (tambores metálicos) manufactured from recycled oil barrels. Venezuelan variants utilize a rhythmic percussion battery based on the bumbac, charrasca, cencerro, and cuatro, while modern adaptations incorporate keyboards, electric basses, and horn sections.
sections.costume_and_setting: Calypso performances historically center around seasonal 'calypso tents' and large-scale Carnival celebrations. Performers and participants wear vibrant Carnival costumes, and competition winners traditionally join pageantry winners in the annual costume parade on Carnival Monday.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Calypso serves as a vital medium for sociopolitical commentary, news dissemination, and protest against authoritarian colonial culture. Singers use the genre to lampoon politicians, critique economic inequalities, and voice community concerns during Carnival and national elections.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical and contemporary figures include Attila the Hun, Roaring Lion, Lord Invader, Lord Kitchener, Mighty Sparrow, Calypso Rose, and Harry Belafonte, who popularized the genre globally in the 1950s.
sections.regional_variants: Regional expressions include benna in Antigua and Barbuda, spouge in Barbados, Dominica cadence-lypso, Venezuelan calipso de El Callao, Jamaican mento, and soca music.
sections.lineage: Derived from West African Kaiso, French Creole belair, and calinda stick-fighting chants, calypso subsequently influenced international genres like ska and evolved directly into soca music.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is rooted in Anishinaabe oral tradition, attributed to Pukawiss, who used movement to teach animal behaviors. The modern competitive form was established in the 1930s by Tony White Cloud, who utilized multiple hoops to create a stylized performance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dancer uses up to 28 hoops to create shapes. Movements are either clockwise or counterclockwise, determined by the dancer's cosmology. The dancer takes small, restrained steps while rapidly manipulating the hoops to form appendages like wings or tails.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music typically features a drumbeat and flute. The tempo varies; some dancers perform to extremely fast songs, while others use a slower drumbeat to accommodate more complex hoop arrangements.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers often wear traditional regalia. Hoops are decorated with tape and paint, often in four colors representing the four directions. Performances occur at powwows, formal competitions, and public stages.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The hoop symbolizes the never-ending cycle of life. In White Mountain Apache tradition, it was historically used in healing ceremonies, such as those for lightning-struck individuals. Today, it is a celebrated cultural performance.
sections.notable_figures: Tony White Cloud (founder of modern hoop dance), Eddie Swimmer (first World Champion), Quentin Pipestem, Jackie Bird, Ginger Sykes, Jasmine Pickner, Lisa Odjig, and Kevin Locke.
sections.regional_variants: While pan-Indian in nature, specific tribal traditions like those of the White Mountain Apache emphasize healing, whereas modern competitive hoop dance focuses on technical speed and artistic innovation.
sections.lineage: The dance is a descendant of traditional storytelling and healing dances, evolving into the modern competitive form seen today.

claims.text: Native American Hoop Dance is a form of individual dance, performed as a show dance in many tribes.
Most of the hoop dances in tribes across North America belong to modern hoop dance, which was invented in 1930.
The dancer usually takes small steps when performing the dance.
The hoops symbolizes the 'never-ending cycle of life,' having no beginning and no end.
The first World Hoop Dance Competition was held at the New Mexico State Fair in 1991.
In 1994, Jackie Bird became the first woman to compete in the Hoop Dance World Championships.
The hoop dance is a living tradition, with annual competitions held at the Heard Museum.

sections.origins_and_history: El vito is a traditional folk song, dance, and music genre of Andalusia with origins tracing back to the sixteenth century. Its name alludes to Saint Vitus, the patron of dancers, and the lively dance associated with him. Developed in the nineteenth century as a bolero-style dancing song, the tradition experienced a major mid-to-twentieth-century revival in Córdoba led by instructor Maruja Cazalla after it had fallen into local oblivion.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is traditionally performed by women who wear jackets and brimmed hats. The physical execution incorporates specific steps drawn from the art of bullfighting, framed by a fast and animated character. Detailed footwork counts and spatial formations are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The melody is played fast in a 3/8 time signature. It utilizes the harmonic minor scale for ascending motives and the phrygian mode for descending motives, resulting in an harmonic accompaniment based on the Andalusian cadence. Instrumentation includes guitar and castanets as featured in traditional recordings.
sections.costume_and_setting: The typical costume for performers includes a jacket and a brimmed hat. The thematic setting often reflects Cordobese culture, traditionally depicting a woman from Córdoba traveling to Seville to observe bullfights.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: El vito is sung with lyrics that can be humorous or serious. It has served multiple societal functions beyond folk dancing, including use as a political anthem during the Spanish Civil War ("El Quinto Regimiento") and controversially as a processional march for Holy Week in Córdoba.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical and artistic figures include Maruja Cazalla, who revived the dance in Córdoba; her mentor Rita Fragero; composer Fernando J. Obradors; violinist Pablo de Sarasate; zarzuela composer Mariano Soriano Fuertes; jazz artists John Coltrane and Charlie Haden; and processional march composer Rafael Wals Dantas.
sections.regional_variants: While broadly Andalusian in origin, El vito became specifically associated with Córdoba during the mid-to-late twentieth century following its local revival.
sections.lineage: El vito is classified as a traditional folk dance and music genre of Andalusia, closely linked in its nineteenth-century development to the bolero form.

sections.origins_and_history: Mak yong originated in the Pattani Kingdom and spread to Kelantan and Kedah over 200 years ago. Passed down orally among villagers, it is estimated to be at least 800 years old. It was patronized by the Kelantan Sultanate until the 1920s. In 1991, Kelantan banned mak yong for its animist elements and women's clothing, but the ban was lifted in 2019.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances open with an offering (semah kampung) followed by dancing, acting, and improvised dialogues across three-hour shows over several nights. Most roles are performed by women, featuring the Pak Yong (king), a queen, palace girls, and male jesters. A group called Jong Dongdang performs songs and dances between chapters.
sections.music_and_instruments: The orchestra features the rebab (a three-stringed spiked lute), gendang (double-headed barrel drums), a pair of gongs (tetawak), serunai (flute), keduk drums, and kesi (small cymbals). Its singing and musical repertoire are distinct and unique to the region.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances traditionally use elaborate costumes where the lead Pak Yong dresses like a king. In villages, performances are held on temporary open stages built of wood and palm leaves, with the audience sitting on three sides and the orchestra on the fourth.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Mak yong served as entertainment, harvest thanksgiving, and healing rituals (such as mak yong mak puteri involving trance-dancing and spirit possession). It acts as a mystical conduit to the spirit world and honors teachers and graduates.
sections.notable_figures: The late Cik Ning was a leading mak yong performer in the 1980s. Long Abdul Ghaffar supported the art in 1923 by building Kampung Temenggung on palace grounds, an effort later continued by Khatijah Awang's Seri Temenggong group.
sections.regional_variants: Variations include Makyong United (Pattani, Yala, Narathiwat), Makyong Kelantan, Makyong Kedah, Makyong Mar (Perlis and Satun), Makyong Riau (Indonesia), Field Makyong (Medan, Indonesia), and Makyong Kalimantan (Indonesia).
sections.lineage: Stories are derived from Kelantan or Patani mythology, including tales like 'Anak Raja Gondang' originating from Buddhist Jataka tales.

sections.origins_and_history: Sean-nós dance represents an older, informal style of solo Irish dancing documented by historians and ethnomusicologists. The term 'sean-nós' was formally applied to the dance form in 1976, distinguishing it from newer competitive stepdance forms.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance features low-to-the-ground footwork, improvised steps, and a percussive batter that emphasizes the musical beat. Dancers perform solo or take turns in small groups without physical contact, keeping arms loose and natural.
sections.music_and_instruments: Accompaniment is provided by a lively traditional Irish band, featuring instruments like the fiddle and accordion. Standard traditional tunes such as McCleod's reel and New Mown Meadows frequently accompany the performance.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear casual everyday clothing without standardized costuming. Traditionally, performances take place on tight wooden surfaces such as a door taken off its hinges, a table, a barrel, or a stool.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed informally at pub sessions, folk festivals, and community gatherings, as well as specialized events and competitions like Oireachtas na Samhna and Comórtas Damhsa Chóilín Sheáin Dharach.
sections.notable_figures: Figures such as Johnny Connolly, Maldon Meehan, and Ronan Regan are noted in connection with the living tradition and preservation of sean-nós dancing.
sections.regional_variants: The dance features regional stylistic subtypes, notably separated into Connemara-style and Munster-style traditions within the western Irish Gaeltacht.
sections.lineage: Sean-nós dance is considered the historical predecessor that influenced modern competitive Irish stepdance as well as forms like North American tap dance.

sections.origins_and_history: The Dances of Universal Peace were first formulated by Samuel L. Lewis, also known as Sufi Ahmed Murad Chisti. The very first dance took place on 16 March 1968 in San Francisco, California. The original dances were strongly influenced by Samuel Lewis's spiritual relationships with modern dance pioneer Ruth St. Denis and Sufi master Hazrat Inayat Khan. Sufi practices such as Sema and The Whirling Dervishes provided clear influences, alongside Lewis's background as a Rinzai Zen master. Originally performed at camps and alternative meetings, the movement expanded into schools, prisons, hospices, and holistic centers. The International Network for the Dances of Universal Peace was founded in 1982 by Neil Douglas-Klotz and Tasnim Fernandez, and the network now has members in 28 countries.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Five to 500 dancers stand in a circle, often around a leader and musicians with acoustic instruments in the center. All dances are participatory and spectating is somewhat discouraged because joy is the goal. Dances are facilitated by a dance leader who often plays a drum, guitar, flute, or other stringed instrument. Each dance is taught afresh at each gathering, allowing dancers of all levels and children to follow along. Many dances feature choreographed movements, steps, and gestures encouraging dancers to explore deeper mystical meanings.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music relies on chants put to traditional, contemporary, or occasionally improvised melodies using inspirational poetry, quotes, and sacred phrases. Facilitators play acoustic instruments such as drums, guitars, flutes, or other stringed instruments in the center of the circle. A wide range of languages are deliberately employed, including Arabic, Aramaic, English, Hawaiian, Hebrew, Persian, and Sanskrit.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dances were originally performed at camps and meetings with a distinctly New Age and alternative feel. Over time, they have increasingly been offered in diverse places of worship and more secular places such as schools, colleges, prisons, hospices, residential homes for those with special needs, and holistic health centers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The intention of the DUP is to raise consciousness and promote peace between diverse religions. Dance leaders tend to believe peace can be promoted through experiencing the same One Joy through diverse dance steps, chants, and languages. Dancing is seen as an opportunity to develop participants' spiritual awareness, hand-eye-body coordination, and competency in harmonizing with others.
sections.notable_figures: Samuel L. Lewis (Sufi Ahmed Murad Chisti) formulated the dances. Ruth St. Denis and Hazrat Inayat Khan influenced Lewis's work. Neil Douglas-Klotz and Tasnim Fernandez founded the International Network for the Dances of Universal Peace in 1982 and became leading exponents.
sections.regional_variants: The dances have developed into a global movement with members in 28 countries. Neil Douglas-Klotz's creation of dances using the Aramaic words of Jesus has entered many alternative and mainstream religious circles.
sections.lineage: The tradition is of North American Sufic origin, drawing significant influence from Sufi practices such as Sema and The Whirling Dervishes, modern dance pioneers like Ruth St. Denis, and Rinzai Zen teachings.
